name: Behdeinkhlam
tagline: A Pnar festival where tall logs and tall rots are carried to a muddy pool to drive away disease.
facts: Festival of the Pnar (Jaintia) people, held in July
Name means driving away plague or disease, from beh dein (drive away) and khlam (plague)
Biggest celebrations are at Jowai and Tuber Kmai
Climax at the Aitnar pool, where polished logs are plunged
art: Behdeinkhlam is the most important festival in the life of the Jaintia, or Pnar, people, according to the Meghalaya arts and culture department. Its name is explained as driving away (beh dein) disease or plague (khlam). It is held in July, after the sowing season, and is linked to prayers for health and a good harvest.

A week before, a pig is sacrificed to the thunder deity. Priests ring a brass bell through the town. Tall polished tree trunks are felled in a preserved forest and brought back to the town with drumming and dancing. Men beat the roofs of houses with bamboo poles to drive out evil spirits, according to Wikipedia.

Youth groups build rots, tall structures of bamboo, coloured paper and tinsel. The government page gives their height as 30 to 40 feet. Groups compete to make the tallest and most artistic. On the last afternoon the rots are carried to Aitnar, a dammed pool with a low brick wall around it. The polished logs are thrown into the water, and men try to balance on them.

Wikipedia also records games during the festival, such as a football-like game with a wooden ball, and a tug of war over a log across a muddy trench. It says women do not dance and instead offer food to the spirits of their forefathers. The government page says dancing takes place during the log processions. People in costume dance to drums around Aitnar, Wikipedia says.
artist: The festival belongs to the Pnar who follow the traditional faith, called Niamtre. Religious leaders called Daloi perform rites with offerings to clans and ancestors. Young men visit homes with priests on the fourth day to drive out evil spirits, and households offer them rice beer, according to the government page.
Rot builders are youth groups from the localities of Jowai and nearby. I found no named individual builders or dancers in the sources I read.
place: Jowai is the headquarters of West Jaintia Hills, at about 1,220 metres and roughly 64 km from Shillong, according to the arts and culture page. The four stones of the deities can still be seen at the corners of the town. Tuber Kmai is the other large site.
Aitnar, in Jowai, is the amphitheatre-like pool where the festival ends. News reports describe thousands of people gathering.

history.what: The government page says the festival began after a great famine, when the deity U Mokhai asked people to hold a community festival after sowing.
Wikipedia says the festival was also linked to celebrating the end of cholera. The two accounts are not the same, and I found no date for either.
Held each July, in the Jaintia calendar months given on the arts and culture page as June to July.
Jowai and Tuber Kmai draw large crowds, including visitors. I did not find any UNESCO status for it.

future: Training: young men learn rot building and ritual roles from elders each year.
Livelihood: bamboo, paper and tinsel purchases and visitors bring some income to Jowai.
Materials: tall trunks come from a preserved forest. Protecting that grove matters for the festival.
Documentation: the festival has rites by locality, and a careful record of each, made with the Daloi, would help.
Protection: crowds and tourism need managing so that the sacred rites stay with the people who hold them.

name: Bhangra and Giddha
tagline: The men's drum-driven harvest dance and the women's clapping circle of sung verses.
facts: Bhangra: tied to the Baisakhi harvest, led by the dhol drum
Giddha: women's circle dance, sung verses called boli
Giddha needs no dhol: women clap the rhythm
Bhangra's stage form developed in the 1950s
art: Bhangra is a folk dance of Punjab, traditionally linked to the harvest festival of Vaisakhi or Baisakhi in April. Its beat comes from the dhol, a double-headed drum played with a heavy stick on one side and a lighter one on the other. Short songs called boliyan go with the dance.

Giddha is a women's folk dance. A lead woman sings a boli, and the circle repeats the refrain. Wikipedia says the verses tell of women's lives, and that unlike other Punjabi dances giddha needs no dhol: women clap the rhythm while elder women sing in the background.
Traditional giddha costume was a bright salwar kameez or ghagra with jewellery and a tikka. Giddha is danced at festive and social occasions.
The two are often called the men's and women's dance. Gibb Schreffler, cited by Wikipedia, writes that calling giddha the women's counterpart of bhangra is not entirely accurate.
artist: These are community dances, so most dancers are unnamed villagers. In the 1950s, Wikipedia says, a troupe from the Deepak family of Sunam and the dhol player Bhana Ram Sunami were among the first big developers of bhangra on stage.
Bhangra was long seen as a men's dance, and its use by women is described in the same source as a more recent change that some find contested.
place: Wikipedia links bhangra's older home to Sialkot district and nearby Majha areas such as Gurdaspur and Gujranwala. After 1947 migrants from West Punjab helped carry it into East Punjab through cultural shows and campuses.
One source cited by the dance's summaries places giddha's roots in the Malwa region of Punjab. We did not open that source, so treat it as unverified here.
Bhangra has since spread across the Punjabi diaspora and mixed with other music styles.

history.what: The exact origin of bhangra as a dance is not well documented. Giddha is said to come from an older ring dance of Punjab (Claude Conyers).
Both are linked in tradition to harvest and festival times.
Partition moved performers across Punjab. Schreffler describes how Punjabi folk dances were promoted as cultural symbols after Partition.
The Maharaja of Patiala asked for a staged bhangra performance, according to Wikipedia.
Competitions were held in Patiala and a stage style took shape.
Bhangra music grew abroad, and women's participation grew with it.

future: Teach the older village forms (including boliyan) as well as the stage style.
Record elder women who know traditional giddha boliyan, with their consent.
Pay dhol players and teachers fairly for school and college programmes.
Support community and girls' groups in giddha, not only in competition.
Document regional differences between Majha, Malwa and Doaba styles.

name: Bharatanatyam
tagline: A dance of fixed lines, bent knees and quick feet, offered to Nataraja, the lord of dance.
facts: Form: solo classical dance with hand gesture, footwork and song
Home: Tamil Nadu, with roots in temple and court dance
Name Bharatanatyam adopted in 1932 for the older sadir
Recognised by Sangeet Natak Akademi as a classical dance
art: Bharatanatyam comes from Tamil Nadu. It joins nritta (pure dance, with no story), nritya (dance that tells a poem through expression) and, in dance-dramas, natya. The dancer keeps the knees bent and turned out, the back straight, and the feet strike the floor in clear rhythm while the hands and eyes speak.

A full recital follows a sequence called the margam, the path. Wikipedia lists it as pushpanjali (an offering of flowers), alarippu (a rhythmic opening), jatiswaram (pure dance set to melody), shabdam (the first piece with words), varnam (the longest and central piece), padam (a quiet song of feeling), tillana (a lively close) and a blessing, shlokam or mangalam. Sources count and name the parts a little differently.

Most pieces are sung in Tamil, Telugu, Kannada or Sanskrit to Carnatic music. A nattuvanar keeps time with cymbals and calls out the dance syllables. A mridangam, violin, flute and singer complete the group.

The form is danced for Nataraja, Shiva as lord of dance. At Chidambaram, the temple's gateways carry carved panels of dance poses. Wikipedia notes that the southern gateway, dated to about the 12th century, shows 108 poses described as karanas in the Natya Shastra, a Sanskrit text on the arts whose date scholars place anywhere from around 500 BCE to 500 CE.
artist: Before the 20th century the dance was known as sadir or dasi attam and was kept by hereditary families of women dancers, often called devadasis, together with male teachers and musicians called nattuvanars. The families passed the art from mother to daughter and from teacher to pupil. Scholar Davesh Soneji argues that court and temple dancing in this form took shape in the late 16th or 17th century under the Nayaka rulers; other writers trace it further back, and this is still debated.

The Thanjavur Quartet were four brothers, Chinnayya, Ponnayya, Sivanandam and Vadivelu. They served Serfoji II at Thanjavur and later worked in other courts, such as Travancore and Mysore. They are credited with giving the repertoire its present shape, including the order of the margam. Only Ponnayya's years (1804 to 1864) are given in the source I read.

In the late 19th and early 20th centuries, reformers and the colonial government attacked temple dancing. Wikipedia dates an anti-dance movement from 1892 and a ban on temple dancing in the Madras Presidency from 1910. Many hereditary families lost their work and their standing, and the dancers' own voices were largely left out of the public debate. In 1932 the Madras Music Academy took up the name Bharatanatyam in place of sadir, a change linked to E. Krishna Iyer and Rukmini Devi Arundale.

Rukmini Devi Arundale, with George Arundale, set up Kalakshetra in Adyar, Chennai, in January 1936. It became an institution that trained dancers from outside the hereditary families and shaped a distinct style. It was recognised by an Act of Parliament as an Institute of National Importance in 1994. Many other gurus and schools carry other styles of the form, and the hereditary families, including Balasaraswati's family, are part of this story too.
Our approach: tell the history of the devadasi families with care and without judgement, and include voices from within those families wherever we can.
place: Bharatanatyam belongs to the Kaveri delta and the Tamil country. Thanjavur, with the Brihadisvara temple and the Maratha court of the 18th and early 19th centuries, was the base of the Quartet. Chidambaram, farther north, is the home of the Nataraja temple, where the dance is part of the sculpture.

Temples in Tamil Nadu were large centres of worship, land, music and craft. Dancers and musicians were attached to temples and later also to courts. This long association is the reason the art is tied so closely to Shiva and to the temple calendar.

In the 20th century the centre of gravity moved to Chennai (then Madras). The Madras Music Academy, Kalakshetra and the December music and dance season are now the main platform, while the form is also taught in cities around India and abroad.

history.what: The Natya Shastra and the Tamil epic Silappatikaram are often cited as early sources for Indian dance. Scholars disagree on their dates and on how direct the link to Bharatanatyam is.
Wikipedia dates the Chidambaram southern gateway with its 108 karana panels to about this time.
Davesh Soneji places the rise of court and temple dance in its present form in the Nayaka period. Other scholars hold a different view.
The Thanjavur Quartet work at the court of Serfoji II and shape the repertoire. Exact years of the four brothers are not agreed in the sources I read.
An anti-dance movement begins, according to Wikipedia.
The Madras Presidency bans temple dancing, according to Wikipedia.
At the Madras Music Academy, the name Bharatanatyam is proposed for the art once called sadir.
Rukmini Devi Arundale and George Arundale found Kalakshetra in Adyar, Chennai.
The Madras Devadasis (Prevention of Dedication) Act is passed, ending dedication of girls to temples. I could not check the exact wording in the sources I read.
Kalakshetra is recognised as an Institute of National Importance by an Act of Parliament.

future: Support hereditary teaching families, including nattuvanars and musicians, with fair teaching posts and honoraria.
Document the repertoire of different banis (Pandanallur, Vazhuvoor, Kalakshetra and others) on video with notation and the teachers' own words.
Open scholarships so that children from families without any dance background can train for the full years it takes.
Pay accompanying musicians and nattuvanars fairly for each recital, as they are often paid far less than the dancer.
Publish the history of devadasi communities with their own voices and keep it in a public archive.
Take dance to small towns and temple festivals, not only to city halls in the December season.

name: Bihu Dance and the Dhol
tagline: A drum, a buffalo-horn pipe and a spring festival that Assam dances to.
facts: Three Bihus: Rongali (April), Kongali (October), Bhogali (January)
Dhol, pepa (buffalo horn) and gogona (bamboo) are key instruments
Assam Bihu Dhol received a GI tag in March 2024
11,304 dancers and drummers performed together in Guwahati in April 2023
art: Bihu is a festival unique to Assam, and its dance and drum are what most people think of first. Wikipedia lists three Bihus in a year. Rongali or Bohag Bihu falls in mid-April, marks the Assamese New Year and spring, and lasts about seven days. Kongali or Kati Bihu, around mid-October, is quiet and solemn, tied to the growing paddy, with earthen lamps lit in the fields. Bhogali or Magh Bihu, in mid-January, is a harvest festival of feasts and bonfires.

The dance belongs mostly to Rongali Bihu. Mukoli Bihu is danced in open fields by young unmarried men and women, and Jeng Bihu is performed by women only. The modern stage form is said to derive from the Faat Bihu dance of Dhakuakhana in Lakhimpur, according to the sources Wikipedia cites.

The dhol is the heartbeat. It is a drum played with a stick and by hand. The Assam Tribune describes dhols made from a wooden barrel covered with animal skin, cow or goat, and says one dhol takes at least three to four days to make. Alongside it come the pepa, made of buffalo horn, and the gogona, made of bamboo.

The drummer sets the rhythm and the dancers follow it. In April 2023, the Assam government staged a single-venue performance at the Indira Gandhi Athletic Stadium in Guwahati with 11,304 dancers and drummers. EastMojo reports that Guinness World Records recognised it in two categories, Bihu dance and Bihu dhol.
artist: Bihu has no single founder. It is a community art, danced by villagers and learned by watching and joining in. The dhol player and the dancer are usually from the same village, and many are farmers.

Dhol making is a small-scale craft. The Assam Tribune spoke to Haren Badyakar, whose family at Muktapur near Baihata Chariali has made dhols since the late 1980s. They sold about 40 dhols in the previous year, mostly around Bohag Bihu, and demand is seasonal. He hoped the GI tag would bring state support.

The paper also notes that in villages few boys now learn the dhol while many girls want to learn Bihu dance, though a Guwahati teacher, Rantu Saikia, says more boys are learning each year and not only from the Assamese community.
place: Bihu belongs to the Brahmaputra valley and its farming year. The festivals follow sowing, the growing season and harvest, which is why each Bihu feels so different from the others.

Guwahati is where Bihu moved onto the public stage. Wikipedia says the urban Bihutoli form began in 1962 in Guwahati, promoted by the Guwahati Bihu Sanmilani. Villages and fields remain its older home.

history.what: Wikipedia, citing a 2015 Assamese study, says Bihu may come from the Deori word Bisu, meaning excessive joy.
The Deodhai Buranji records an Ahom attack on the Chutia capital at Sadiya on the first day of Bihu, while people were celebrating.
Ahom king Rudra Singha is said to have patronised Bihu and was the first to celebrate it in the courtyard of Rang Ghar.
Bihutoli, the open-stage urban Bihu, begins in Guwahati.
11,304 dancers and drummers perform at Guwahati; Guinness World Records recognises it.
Assam Bihu Dhol receives a Geographical Indication tag, announced by the Chief Minister on 31 March.

future: Teaching: village and school classes in dhol as well as dance, so that drumming has young learners as well as dancers.
Livelihood: dhol makers earn mostly around Bohag Bihu, so steady orders and support schemes would help them.
Protection: the GI tag is meant to protect the name Assam Bihu Dhol and its makers from imitation.
Documentation: record regional styles of Bihu, from Faat Bihu in Dhakuakhana to Jeng Bihu, with the dancers and drummers themselves.
Materials: record the woods and skins used and where they come from, so makers can plan supply.

name: Bonalu
tagline: Women carry pots of food on their heads to the village mother goddess, to drums.
facts: Honours: Mahankali and other village goddesses
Season: Ashada (about July to August)
Declared a Telangana state festival after 2014
Features: bonam pots, Pothuraju, Ghatam, Rangam
art: Bonalu is a festival of thanks to the mother goddess. Women cook rice with milk and jaggery, put it in a decorated pot and carry it on their heads to the temple. The pot has neem leaves, turmeric, kumkum and a lamp. The name is said to come from bhojanalu, meaning meals.

Dance and drum are at the heart of it. Teenmar drums drive the processions. The Pothuraju, who is seen as the goddess's brother, dances at the front. He is described as bare-chested, smeared with turmeric, with ankle bells and a whip, and he stands for protection.

The Ghatam is a decorated copper pot that stands for the goddess. It is carried through the streets and is later immersed in water. The day after the main offering, at the Ujjaini Mahankali temple, a woman stands on a pot in trance and speaks about the year ahead. This is called Rangam.
Bonalu is celebrated at several temples in the twin cities in turn: the Jagadamba temple at Golconda Fort, the Ujjaini Mahankali temple in Secunderabad, and the Lal Darwaza temple in the Old City.
artist: The festival is made by many people. Women carry the bonam. Drummers and Pothuraju performers lead the processions. Priests carry the Ghatam, and a woman gives the Rangam prophecy.
I did not find a source that names individual performers, so none are named here.
Our approach: record the drummers and Pothuraju performers by name in each temple's procession.
place: Bonalu is best known in Hyderabad and Secunderabad but is also held in towns and villages across Telangana. The Ujjaini Mahankali temple is in Secunderabad, and its Lashkar Bonalu is often described as the most prominent.
The Ghatam procession goes from Lal Darwaza to Nayapul and is immersed in the Musi river, according to Pragyata.

history.what: The South First article links Bonalu to older village goddess traditions that guard against disease.
A popular story says soldiers prayed to Mahakali during a plague in the twin cities and offered thanks when it ended. Sources give 1813 and 1869, so the date is uncertain.
South First says the Telangana government declared Bonalu a state festival after the state was formed. Another source gives 2016 for the declaration.
The state organises Bonalu each year, beginning at Golconda Fort.

future: Training: pass on the drum rhythms and Pothuraju dance to younger people.
Livelihood: fair fees for drummers and dancers during the season.
Materials: keep pots, neem and turmeric supplies local, and keep immersion clean.
Documentation: film and record songs and rhythms at each temple.
Protection: protect the oral and ritual knowledge held by priests and women of the community.

name: Cheraw (Bamboo Dance)
tagline: Dancers step in and out of clapping bamboo poles, and the poles are the music.
facts: Form: bamboo pole dance of the Mizo
Music: the beat of the poles, sometimes with gongs and drums
Usual group: six to eight dancers (Wikipedia)
2010: Guinness record of 10,736 dancers in Aizawl
art: In Cheraw, pairs of long bamboo poles are tapped on the ground and struck together in rhythm. Dancers step between the poles with hops, slides and crossing steps. The tempo and footwork get faster and harder as the dance goes on. Wikipedia says some movements are inspired by swaying trees and flying birds.

Two accounts say men usually handle the poles while women dance between them. Amar Chitra Katha says the poles lie horizontally on the ground, and male dancers clap them together and against the floor in pairs.

The pole beat is the core music. Some modern shows add the khuang drum, darbu gongs and cymbals. Sources describe the women's dress as a vakiria headdress decorated with feathers, a blouse, and a puanchei skirt, mostly in white, red, green and black.
The dance is performed at community gatherings, weddings and festivals, above all at Chapchar Kut in March, which falls after the jhum fields are cleared.
artist: Cheraw belongs to the Mizo as a whole rather than to named masters. It is learned by watching and joining in. One article says elders pass it on informally. I found no named dancers or teachers in the sources I read.
Pole-holders need steady timing so that dancers do not get caught. Dancers learn to enter the gap on the beat. Teamwork is stressed in the accounts I read.
place: Mizoram is a hill state in north-east India. Bamboo grows widely there and is used for houses, baskets and tools. The dance uses a material that is part of everyday life.

Chapchar Kut is a spring festival held in March. Amar Chitra Katha ties its timing to the season when bamboo is cut, dried and burned to clear fields. In Aizawl the festival is held at Lammual, the ground used for the 2010 record.

history.what: Wikipedia and Amar Chitra Katha say the dance is believed to date to the 1st century AD. I could not find evidence behind this. IGNCA says plainly that the origin of Cheraw is uncertain.

One legend, repeated by Amar Chitra Katha, IGNCA and Humans of North East, ties the dance to rites for the soul of a woman who died leaving a newborn child. Sources describe it as a story, not a record.
Humans of North East says the dance moved from mourning to celebration and became linked with farming festivals.
At Chapchar Kut in Aizawl, 10,736 dancers in 671 groups performed for eight minutes, a Guinness-certified record per Open magazine. Amar Chitra Katha gives 10,763; the Open figure is used here.
Amar Chitra Katha says Cheraw was shown at an International Dance Day event in London.

future: Training: teach Cheraw in schools and colleges, as one article suggests, with elders as guides.
Livelihood: pay performers fairly for festival and tourism shows.
Materials: keep bamboo supply and local bamboo skills for poles and dress.
Documentation: film the dance and record elders' stories, including the older ritual meaning.
Protection: involve bodies such as the Sangeet Natak Akademi; one article suggests this, but I found no existing Akademi project.

name: Chhau
tagline: A night-time dance of mock combat, bird and animal gaits and village chores, in three regional styles.
facts: Three styles: Seraikella, Mayurbhanj and Purulia
Masks are used in Seraikella and Purulia, not in Mayurbhanj
Linked to the spring festival Chaitra Parva
Inscribed by UNESCO in 2010
art: Chhau is a dance from eastern India that tells stories from the Mahabharata and Ramayana, local folklore and abstract themes. UNESCO describes its movement as a mix of mock combat, stylised gaits of birds and animals, and movements taken from the daily chores of village housewives.

There are three styles, named for the places where they are kept: Seraikella in Jharkhand, Mayurbhanj in Odisha and Purulia in West Bengal. Seraikella and Purulia dancers wear masks. Mayurbhanj dancers do not, although Sahapedia notes there is evidence that masks were used there in the nineteenth century.

The masks differ. Sahapedia describes Seraikella masks as light, covering the whole face, with small openings for the eyes and nose, and often calm, stylised expressions. Early ones are said to have been made of bamboo and gourd and later ones of papier-mache. Purulia masks are larger and heavier, with bold faces of gods and demons. The dancer must have strength to perform acrobatics under them.
Performances take place at night in open spaces, with the reed pipes mohuri and shehnai and a range of drums. Chhau is tied to regional festivals, especially the spring festival Chaitra Parva.
Where the name comes from is not settled. Wikipedia lists several suggestions, including the Sanskrit chhaya (shadow) or chadma (disguise) and the Odia chhauni (camp). Treat all of these as guesses.
artist: UNESCO says Chhau is taught to male dancers, from families of traditional artists or from local communities. It is learned from a guru, and the dancers come from many social backgrounds, professions and languages.

In Seraikella, Sahapedia and other accounts say the local royal family supported the form and also took part, as dancers and choreographers. In Purulia, Sahapedia says there was no significant royal patronage, and performers come mostly from indigenous communities such as Mura, Bhumij and Kurmi.

Masks are the work of separate craft families. Sahapedia says most Purulia masks are made in Chodra village in Baghmundi. Other press reports name Charida village near Purulia as a mask-making village. I could not confirm the household numbers they quote, so none are given here.

UNESCO warns that industrialisation, economic pressure and new media are reducing community participation. Our approach: name the gurus, musicians and mask makers of each village in every story, and ask them how they want the dance to be shown.
place: The three styles lie across the plateau and forest country where Jharkhand, Odisha and West Bengal meet. Seraikella is a town in Seraikela Kharsawan district, Jharkhand. Baripada is the main town of Mayurbhanj in Odisha. Purulia is the western edge of West Bengal.

This was once a land of small princely and zamindari estates and of forest communities. The dance carries that mix. Scholars link its roots to local martial practices and folk dance. Wikipedia names the Paika (a martial tradition) and Nachni dance as influences, though it does not give dates.
The festival season centres on Chaitra Parva in spring, when whole communities take part. Open village grounds and temple fields are the usual stages.

history.what: UNESCO says Chhau traces back to indigenous dance and martial practices. No firm date is known, and scholars do not agree on how the three styles separated.
The rulers of Seraikella and Mayurbhanj supported the dance at court. Sahapedia notes that the Seraikella royal family also performed and choreographed.
One account dates the Purulia mask tradition to about this time, in the reign of the Baghmundi king Madan Mohan Singh Deo. This comes from a single press report and needs checking.
Chhau was brought to stages outside its villages, in cities and abroad. Dates and names of early tours should be checked in Sangeet Natak Akademi records.

State and national institutions began to teach and support the dance. Wikipedia lists a training centre at Baripada founded in 1962. It also gives 1960 for Seraikella, but that entry is unclear about which government set it up, so it is not repeated here.
UNESCO inscribed Chhau on the Representative List of the Intangible Cultural Heritage of Humanity.
Chhau is still danced at Chaitra Parva and other festivals, and masks are sold to visitors. UNESCO notes pressure from changing livelihoods and new media.

future: Fund long guru-shishya training in all three villages, with stipends so that young dancers do not have to leave for wage work.
Support mask makers with fair prices and direct sales, and record their methods in their own words.
Open training to girls and women where communities agree, and listen first to the elders who hold the tradition.
Record full night performances in each style, with the music and songs, and return copies to the villages.
Hold festivals in the home villages, so the income and the pride stay there.
Keep Chaitra Parva a community event, and give visitors clear guidance on how to attend with respect.

name: Chholiya
tagline: Men with swords and shields dance in front of a Kumaoni wedding procession.
facts: Form: sword-and-shield dance with drums and horns
Danced in wedding processions in Kumaon
Dholi drummers are mostly Dalit; other musicians mostly Rajput
Said to be over a thousand years old; not documented
art: Chholiya, also spelled Choliya, is a sword dance of Kumaon. Wikipedia calls it a sword dance that accompanies a marriage procession. It is now also danced on other auspicious occasions.

The dancers move in pairs and groups with swords and shields, and stage mock fights. PARI says only men take part. Wikipedia says they wear white churidar pyjamas, a turban and a chola, carry a triangular red banner called nishana, and put sandalwood paste on the face.

Music comes from the dhol and damau drums and from horns such as the turi and ransingha. PARI and Wikipedia note that the Scottish-style bagpipe, masakbeen, brought by the British, is now part of Chholiya music.
People told PARI that the dance helps ward off evil spirits and protect the couple from bad luck.
artist: PARI reports that the drummers, called dholies, are mostly Dalits. The other musicians and dancers are from several castes, mainly Rajputs. Wikipedia says the dance is performed mainly by the Rajput community at weddings.
The PARI team filmed a performance at a wedding in Baijnath in Bageshwar district. The article names no individual dancers, and I did not find named masters in the sources I read.
The dholies often come from families that have played for weddings over generations. Their work and pay are not described in the sources I read.
place: Chholiya is especially popular in the Kumaon districts of Almora, Bageshwar, Champawat and Pithoragarh. A related form called Hudkeli is danced across the border in Sudurpashchim province, Nepal.
The setting is a hill village wedding: a procession on the steep path, the groom on a horse, and the troupe leading the way.

history.what: Wikipedia and PARI both say the dance is over a thousand years old and linked to the warrior Kshatriya groups of Kumaon, when marriages were said to be made at sword-point. Wikipedia flags this as lightly sourced, so treat it as a tradition.
Wikipedia says the Chand kings united the native Kshatriyas from about the 10th century and that immigrant Rajputs adopted hill customs. This is a general claim, not a dated source for the dance.
The bagpipe was introduced by the British and taken into the music.
Chholiya is still danced at weddings and at cultural festivals in Kumaon.

future: Training: workshops for young dancers and for dholi drummers, with senior performers teaching.
Livelihood: fair payment for dholi families, and bookings outside the wedding season.
Materials: keep swords, shields and costumes made and repaired locally.
Documentation: record the nine named forms Wikipedia lists with their makers and movements.
Protection: honour the dholi musicians as core artists, not as accompanists.

name: Dollu Kunitha
tagline: A drum dance of the Kuruba Gowdas, where dancers carry the dollu on their bodies and beat it in circles.
facts: Form: drum dance, linked to Beereshwara (Shiva) worship
Community: Kuruba Gowda, Halu Kuruba
Troupe: about 10 to 12 drummers
Shown at Mysuru Dasara and other festivals
art: Dollu Kunitha is a drum dance of Karnataka. Kunitha means dance. The dollu is a large double-headed drum. Dancers hang it from the body and beat it as they move.

A troupe usually has 10 to 12 drummers. They form a circle or a semicircle. A leader with cymbals stands in the centre and controls the beat. Slow and fast rhythms alternate and the group weaves patterns. Karnataka Tourism says smaller, lighter drums now let more people take part.

Costume is simple. Wikipedia, citing Karnataka Tourism, says the upper body is usually bare and a black sheet is tied over the lower garment. Other instruments such as cymbals, trumpets and a flute may join the drums.
Karnataka Tourism says the dance appears at festivals such as the Karaga procession, Mysuru Dasara and temple car festivals.
artist: The dance is linked to the Kuruba Gowdas, and to the Halu Kuruba in Shimoga, according to Wikipedia. It belongs to the worship of Beereshwara, a form of Shiva. In Beereshwara temples a dollu hangs from the ceiling and is beaten whenever worship is offered.

The origin story comes from an oral tradition called the Halumatha Purana or Kuruba Purana. A demon named Dolla swallows Shiva. Shiva tears him open and makes a drum from the skin for his devotees, the Halu Kurubas. This is a community legend, not a dated history.

Women were traditionally not drummers, because the drum is heavy. Sahapedia describes Choodamani Ramachandra of Sagara, Shivamogga, as the first woman to perform and teach Dollu Kunitha. She learned from a temple drummer named Ramappa, and trained for almost two years. She founded Snehasagara Mahila Mandala, a troupe of about a dozen women that has performed in India and abroad.
place: Sources place the form in North Karnataka. One account names Dharwad, Haveri, Gadag and Belagavi. Wikipedia also notes it among the Halu Kuruba of Shimoga. Sources differ on exact limits of its home area.
Today the dance is seen across the state at fairs and processions. Women's troupes such as the one in Sagara show that it is no longer only a men's art.

history.what: The Halumatha Purana tells how Shiva's drum was made from the demon's skin. No date is given.
Dollu is beaten in Beereshwara temples whenever worship is offered, according to Wikipedia.
The dance moves from temple and village ritual to state festivals and stage shows.
Choodamani Ramachandra founds a women's troupe in Sagara. Sahapedia gives no founding year.

future: Keep teaching young drummers within Kuruba communities, with fees for senior drummers who teach.
Help troupes buy or share drums. Sahapedia notes that one women's troupe rented its drum at a daily price.
Pay troupes fairly when they perform at state festivals.
Record dance patterns, drum rhythms and the Kuruba Purana with the communities' consent.
Support women's troupes so training does not depend on one teacher.

name: Fugdi and Dhalo
tagline: Women in rows and circles, singing their own songs, with no drum.
facts: Both are women's dances of Goa and the Konkan
Dhalo: held in the month of Pausha, over about a week
Fugdi: danced in circles with clapping and spinning, usually without instruments
Fugdi is also danced before Ganesha at Ganesh Chaturthi
art: Dhalo is a ritual dance of women. Wikipedia says it is held for about a week in the Hindu month of Pausha, at the start of winter, from the full moon to the sixth day of the waning moon, and is a prayer for the protection of the household. Twelve to 24 women dance in two rows facing each other, with arms linked, moving forward and back while they sing. The dance takes place on an open ground called the mand. The last night is the most important and goes on until dawn.

The Gomantak Times describes dhalo as linked to the fertility of the earth, with dancers circling a heap of earth that stands for Mother Earth. Songs are in Konkani or Marathi and are about religion and daily life. Wikipedia says they were traditionally about Radha and Krishna, and later include episodes from the Ramayana and Mahabharata.

Fugdi is a group dance of women. Dancers stand in a circle, clap, sing and spin. Usually there is no instrument, only the songs. Many songs are made by the women themselves and speak of family life, rivalries and people. Wikipedia lists variants such as Kalashi fugdi, danced with water pots near the mouth, and Katti fugdi, with coconut shells struck together.
The two are linked: fugdi is danced during dhalo, and before Ganesha at Ganesh Chaturthi. Sources say dhalo is slower, but one of them marks that as needing a citation.
artist: The dancers are village women of many ages. Wikipedia says dhalo includes unmarried women, married women and widows, guided by experienced women, and names communities such as Kunbi, Bhandari, Nayak, Gabit and Gawdi. The Christian-Kunbi community also keeps it. In Kunbi and Gavda communities men also join fugdi.

A Herald Goa report on Sarvan village in Bicholim says the women dance for seven nights, wear the nine-yard saree and may be fined for missing a night. We did not find named individual dancers in sources we read.
place: Dhalo is described in many Goan villages. The Herald report focuses on Sarvan in Bicholim taluka. Fugdi is found in Goa and across the Konkan, and the Kalashi form is especially common in Sattari, per Wikipedia.
The mand, an open village ground near the temple, is the stage. Dances begin with an offering to the village deity.

history.what: We found no dated origin. Both dances are described as old village traditions, handed down by women.
Dhalo is still held in villages such as Sarvan, per the Herald Goa report.

future: Record dhalo songs and their singers, since they pass by memory.
Support village groups to keep the full week of dhalo, not only short stage versions.
Teach girls and young women the songs and steps in schools and village clubs.
Pay dancers fairly for festival and tourism shows.
Keep the festival open to all communities that practise the dance.

name: Garba
tagline: Nine nights of circling a lamp, clapping and singing to the goddess.
facts: Danced during Navaratri, in honour of the divine feminine, Shakti
Dancers circle a lamp or an image of the goddess
Inscribed by UNESCO in 2023 as Garba of Gujarat
Open to people of every group
art: Garba is a devotional dance from Gujarat, performed in the festival of Navaratri, the nine nights that honour Shakti, the divine feminine. UNESCO describes dancers moving in a circle around a perforated clay pot holding a lamp, or around an image of the goddess Amba.
The steps are simple. Dancers move in a ring, singing and clapping, and the tempo rises until the circle is whirling. Larger gatherings form several rings turning in different directions.

The lamp in a pot is central. Wikipedia explains the word garba as coming from the Sanskrit garbha, meaning womb, and reads the lit pot as a symbol of life. That reading rests on limited sources, so take it as one interpretation.

Garba is often named with dandiya raas, a related dance in which dancers strike pairs of sticks. The two have mixed in modern festivals. Traditional music uses the dhol and other percussion, and today recorded and live bands are common. Women usually wear the chaniya choli, and men the kediyu.
UNESCO stresses that it is a shared practice, learned by watching and joining in, and that it brings together people of different classes, genders and religions.
artist: Garba has few professional performers in the usual sense. The dancers are neighbours, families and whole mohallas. UNESCO lists a wide set of bearers: dancers, musicians, craftspeople and religious figures.

Singers and drummers lead each night, and many gather from the same neighbourhoods each year. The craft side includes potters who make the garbo pots and tailors, embroiderers and mirror-work artisans who prepare festival clothes. I did not find named individuals in the sources I consulted, so none are listed.
The practice passes on through participation, in homes, societies and temples, and through schools, NGOs and the media, according to UNESCO.
Our approach: record the singers, drummers and potters of each place by name, with their consent, and avoid treating garba only as a large paid event.
place: Garba belongs to Gujarat, a state on the western coast, with farmland in the east and Saurashtra and Kachchh in the west. Navaratri falls in the autumn, after the monsoon. Villages gather in a courtyard or chowk, and cities now hold large ground events.

Vadodara is often named for its big Navaratri celebrations, and Ahmedabad also draws crowds. Ambaji, in north Gujarat, is a major shrine of the goddess Amba. These are well-known places, but the dance is found in nearly every part of the state.
The festival is also kept by Gujarati communities across India and abroad. In the cities it has become a large seasonal economy of clothes, music and event organising.

history.what: Folk dances around a lamp or a pot have long been part of Gujarat's goddess worship. I found no firm date for when garba took its present form.
Garba spread from villages to city neighbourhoods and societies. The Wikipedia article has no firm history section, so details of this change need further research.
Wikipedia notes that universities began to hold garba competitions from about this time.

UNESCO inscribed Garba of Gujarat on the Representative List of the Intangible Cultural Heritage of Humanity at the 18th session of its committee in Kasane, Botswana, in early December. Press reports call it India's 15th element on the list.
Garba is danced in homes, societies and large grounds, and it is a regular part of Gujarati identity in India and abroad.

future: Support village and mohalla Navaratri groups, so that the community form stays alive beside large ticketed events.
Record the traditional garba songs, with singers' names and local variants, in an open archive in Gujarati and English.
Pay potters, tailors and embroiderers fairly for festival work, and name them in public materials.
Keep events safe and open for women and for people of all communities, with clear rules and access.
Teach garba in schools as part of Gujarat's cultural history, not just as a competition.
Plan big events with attention to noise, waste and crowd safety near neighbourhoods.

name: Garia Dance
tagline: Young dancers, flute and drum greet the god of the sowing season.
facts: Danced at Garia Puja in mid-April (Baisakh)
Performed by Tripuri and Jamatia, with other groups also taking part
A bamboo pole represents the deity Garia
Instruments reported: sumui flute, kham drum, sarinda
art: Garia dance is performed during Garia Puja, a festival of the Tripuri, Reang, Jamatia and Noatia peoples that marks the start of sowing and prays for a good harvest. A tribal priest, the Ochai, first worships Baba Garia, and the dance follows, with men and women taking part, per the NVLI entry.

Humans of Northeast describes the dance as performed by young boys and girls in bright costumes, in rhythmic formations to drums, flutes and bamboo percussion. It names the sumui (flute), kham (drum) and sarinda (string instrument). This is a blog source and its detail is not confirmed elsewhere.
A bamboo pole stands for the deity, decorated with flowers, cotton threads and cloth. News on Air reports devotees offering decorated bamboo poles, flowers and fruit.
artist: The dancers are community youth, learning in the village from elders. We found no named dancers or teachers in the sources we read.
Sources differ on who dances. The NVLI entry says Tripuri and Jamatia; Humans of Northeast names Tripuri, Reang, Jamatia and Noatia as celebrating the puja.
place: Garia Puja is held across Tripura. News on Air reports the main state-level celebration at Garjantoli in Teliamura, organised by the Jamatia Hoda, with community pujas in Agartala.
People from both tribal and non-tribal communities take part, and the festival is described as spreading messages of harmony.

history.what: We did not find a reliable source on when the dance began. It is tied to jhum cultivation and the sowing season.
Held in the first week of Baisakh in mid-April; sources differ slightly on the exact day.
Humans of Northeast says cock sacrifice is traditional, while urban celebrations may be symbolic.

future: Training: youth classes in dance and in making the sumui and kham.
Livelihood: instrument makers and costume weavers can find steady work through festivals.
Materials: bamboo supply for poles and flutes.
Documentation: record songs, steps and meanings with Ochai priests and elders.
Protection: include the dance in state and national lists of intangible heritage.

name: Ghoomar
tagline: Veiled women spin until their skirts open like flowers.
facts: Form: women's circle dance
Name from ghoomna, to twirl
Instruments: dhol, shehnai
Danced at weddings and festivals
art: Ghoomar is a folk dance of Rajasthan, also spelled ghumar. Its name comes from ghoomna, to twirl. Women dance in a circle, spinning slowly so that the wide skirt spreads out, and move in and out of the ring.

The usual dress is a choli, a wide ghagra or chaniya, and a thin veil drawn over the head and face. Utsavpedia says silver ornaments, kundan jewellery and mirror necklaces are common, cotton is the everyday fabric, and silk or chiffon is used for special days. It adds that the amount of embroidery was traditionally a sign of family wealth.

Wikipedia names dhol and shehnai as the instruments, and songs such as Gorband, Podina and Rumal. Costume and style differ between places such as Udaipur, Kota and Bundi. Near Gujarat the beat is faster and the steps look like garba, and in the Dhaulpur-Karauli area it is slower.

Today Ghoomar is danced at weddings and pre-wedding gatherings, festivals, and at Holi, Diwali and the rains, according to Utsavpedia. By tradition a new bride dances when she is welcomed into her husband's home.
artist: Ghoomar is a community dance more than a stage art, and women are its keepers. Wikipedia says that local women danced it first and that Rajput women of the elite joined later, and that men did not take part in the traditional performance.

Wikipedia says that in 1986 Rajmata Goverdhan Kumari of Santrampur founded the Gangaur Ghoomar Dance Academy to preserve the dance, and that she received the Padma Shri in 2007. We could not confirm this from a second source.
Most of the people who keep Ghoomar alive are not named in print. They are mothers, aunts and neighbours who teach it at weddings and festivals.
place: Utsavpedia places Ghoomar in Marwar, the region around Jodhpur in south-western Rajasthan. Wikipedia says it spread through Rajasthan in the time of the Rajput kings, and is now seen from Jodhpur and Udaipur to Kota, Bundi and beyond.
Rajasthan's hot, dry climate shapes the dress: cotton is preferred, and bright colours stand out against sand and stone. Red and green with gold are favoured because they are linked to prosperity.

history.what: Wikipedia and Utsavpedia say the Bhil tribe developed Ghoomar, as worship of the goddess Sarasvati. Other popular accounts name Parvati. There is no firm date, and these are traditional accounts.
Wikipedia says the Bhils and Rajput kings were often at war until they made peace, and that Rajput women later took up the dance.
The dance became popular across Rajasthan under Rajput rulers, according to Wikipedia.
Gangaur Ghoomar Dance Academy founded by Rajmata Goverdhan Kumari of Santrampur, as Wikipedia reports.
A song titled Ghoomar in the film Padmaavat brought the dance to a national audience, says Wikipedia.

future: Teach the dance in schools and women's groups in its home districts, with elder women as teachers.
Record regional styles (Marwar, Mewar, Hadoti) side by side, with the songs and their meanings.
Pay dancers and teachers for performance and teaching, so that it is not only an unpaid wedding custom.
Support the weavers, embroiderers and silversmiths who make the dress.
Tell the Bhil origin story with the Bhil community, and credit them when it is performed.

name: Ghumura
tagline: A pot-shaped war drum that became a dance of the Kalahandi villages.
facts: Instrument: the ghumura, a pot-shaped drum
Region: Kalahandi and nearby western Odisha
Danced at Nuakhai, Dussehra and other festivals
Forms include circular, semi-circular and animal-themed dances
art: Ghumura is a folk dance of Kalahandi in western Odisha. It is named after the ghumura, a pot-shaped drum. Wikipedia links the name to the ghumuri, a clay water pot used by women.

Dancers form circles, half circles, triangles and squares. Some dances imitate animals, such as the cow-foot and sheep-fighting dances. A competitive form, Ghumura-Ladhei, has rival groups put questions on social and political issues in song.
Groups traditionally gathered at deity shrines during festivals such as Dussehra. The district site says about 18 to 20 artists perform on Nuakhai, Dussehra and other occasions.
artist: Wikipedia says the dance began as war music for soldiers, including the Paikas, and later became leisure for villagers, with royal support. Its caste origins are unclear and it later spread across castes.
The sources disagree on who dances. One calls it male, while another says women from several communities also perform. We have not settled this.
OrissaPOST reports that artistes struggle to make a living from Ghumura, and village groups at Nuakhai, Khandabasa, Chhatar Yatra and Dussehra are declining.
place: Kalahandi lies in southwestern Odisha, bordering Chhattisgarh. Wikipedia places the dance between the Indravati and Mahanadi rivers, with links to Bastar.
Bhawanipatna, Junagarh and Khariar are named as places where groups gathered at shrines.

history.what: Accounts link the drum to the Chandi Purana, the Mahabharata and Ravana. These are traditions and not dated history.
Wikipedia lists claims from prehistoric rock art to the 10th century, and temple carvings at Konark and Bhimeswar as evidence for the 12th century. These claims are not firmly established.
The dance became a leisure pastime for village groups, with royal families as patrons.
The Maa Manikeswari Ghumura Training Centre opened in Bhabanipatana under the state Culture Department and Odisha Sangeet Natak Akademi, with 30 trainees on a stipend.
OrissaPOST reports that the centre closed when government funding stopped.

future: Training: restart the Bhabanipatana centre or an academy, as artistes demand, with fair stipends.
Livelihood: paid festival and school performances so artists can dance full time.
Materials: support drum makers and the supply of skins and clay.
Documentation: record the rhythms, steps and songs from older performers.
Protection: include Ghumura in school and college programmes, as artistes request.

name: Hemis Cham Masks
tagline: Monks in painted masks dance the life of Guru Padmasambhava in the courtyard of Hemis.
facts: Festival: Hemis Tsechu, honouring Guru Padmasambhava
Held at Hemis Monastery, about 45 km from Leh
Dancers: monks, with horns, drums and cymbals
Date: 24-25 June per Ladakh Tourism; it follows the lunar calendar
art: Cham is a masked and costumed dance of Tibetan Buddhism. It is seen as a meditation and an offering, not a stage show, and watching it is believed to bring merit. The old Western label 'devil dance' came from outsiders looking at the costumes.

At Hemis the cham is the heart of the two-day Tsechu. The IGNCA records the order of the dances. On the first day there is a dance of thirteen Black Hat dancers to drive off evil, a dance of sixteen Dakinis around a sacred pole, and the main dance honouring the eight forms of Guru Padmasambhava. Fierce protectors, skeleton-masked Durdag and Herukas follow. A dough figure of Adharma is cut.

On the second day come the Black Hat dance again, a buffalo-masked deity dancing round a painted mandala, and four skeleton-masked dancers who wipe the mandala away. The festival ends with a Laughing Buddha mask and a comic teacher and disciple scene. Two masked jesters open the day and keep the crowd in order.

The music is chants, damaru and drums, conches, long trumpets, cymbals, reed pipes and a handbell. Masks stand for deities and protectors. A Hemis monk quoted in a news feature says the masks stand for peace, compassion and unity. Sources we read do not say who makes the masks or of what, so we do not state it.
artist: The dancers are monks of Hemis, who follow the Drukpa lineage. We found no source that names individual dancers or mask makers, and we do not invent any.

Lay people come in large numbers. A news feature quotes visitors who describe the masks differently: as freedom and insight, as peace and the Guru's blessing, or as a reminder of death that takes away the fear of it. The meaning is personal as well as doctrinal.
place: Hemis Monastery stands on the bank of the Indus, about 45 km from Leh, reached by the Leh-Manali road. Its courtyard is the stage. Hemis is the main seat of the Drukpa lineage in Ladakh.
Cham dances are also held in other Ladakhi monasteries at their own festivals. Hemis is the best known because it falls in summer, when travel to Ladakh is easiest.

history.what: Padmasambhava, also called Guru Rinpoche, is said to have introduced the dances. The IGNCA gives the early 9th century; this is a tradition, not a fixed date.
Wikipedia says the monastery existed before the 11th century.
Hemis was re-established by King Sengge Namgyal, according to Wikipedia.

The IGNCA says the Hemis festival has been held regularly from about this time, in the time of Rgyalsras Mipham Tsewang Rimpoche. Another feature says the mask dance goes back to the time of Ladakh's kings.

Ladakh Tourism lists the festival for 24-25 June. Wikipedia says early June and adds that every twelve years the festival has a larger celebration. Sources differ; the date follows the Tibetan lunar calendar.

future: Fund the monastery's own training of young monks in dance, music and mask care.
Document the dances and their order on film with the monks' consent.
Teach visitors how to watch respectfully, since it is a ritual.
Make sure local families earn from the festival through homestays, food and crafts.
Record who makes and repairs the masks and costumes, and help them continue.

name: Hozagiri Dance
tagline: Dancers balance pitchers and lamps while moving only from the waist down.
facts: Community: Reang (Bru)
Performed by women in teams of four to six
Season: after harvest, around Laxmi Puja
Spelled Hojagiri in many sources
art: Hozagiri, also spelled Hojagiri, is a folk dance of the Reang (Bru) people of Tripura. Young women dance in teams of four to six. They sing as they dance and balance objects such as an earthen pitcher or a bottle on the head, with lamps or plates on the hands. Only the lower half of the body moves.

Humans of Northeast describes it as a thanksgiving after harvest, linked to Laxmi Puja, and as an offering to the goddess Mailuma, who protects crops and households. Wikipedia on the Reang says it depicts the jhum cultivation cycle.

Men play the music. The same feature lists the khamb drum, the sarinda fiddle, flutes and cymbals. Costume is a woven wrap skirt (rignai), bead necklaces, bangles and flowers in the hair. Songs are in the Reang dialect. Details differ between sources.
artist: The best-documented person is Satyaram Reang (1943 to 2 October 2023), known as the Hojagiri Dance Guru. Wikipedia lists the Sangeet Natak Akademi Award in 1986 and the Padma Shri in 2021. A 2021 news report says he opened a school to spread the dance among young people.
Search results differ on other names linked to the dance, including Maniram Reang and Maityaram Reang, and I could not confirm their roles, so they are left out.
place: Hozagiri belongs to the Reang villages of Tripura, where Reang are the second most populous tribe. Many Bru families were displaced from Mizoram from 1997, and settlement has been a long-running issue.
The dance is held after Durga Puja around Laxmi Puja, according to Wikipedia on the Reang.

history.what: No source I read gives a firm date for the origin of Hozagiri.
Satyaram Reang is born.
Satyaram Reang receives the Sangeet Natak Akademi Award.
Violence in Mizoram displaces many Bru into Tripura; community life is disrupted.
Satyaram Reang receives the Padma Shri.
Satyaram Reang dies on 2 October.

future: Training: continue his school model, with village teachers and regular classes for girls.
Livelihood: paid stage and festival performances, and fees for musicians.
Materials: support makers of the khamb drum and sarinda, and of woven costume.
Documentation: record songs in the Reang dialect with elders.
Protection: keep its festival and ritual meaning; stage versions should say where they come from.

pins.label: Reang areas of Dhalai and North Tripura

name: Jhumair and Domkach
tagline: Circle songs of the fields, and the wedding dance that follows the harvest.
facts: Jhumair: song and dance form of the Chota Nagpur plateau
Domkach: a wedding dance in the Nagpuri tradition
Instruments: mandar, dhol, bansi, nagara
Sung in Nagpuri, Kurmali and other languages
art: Jhumair, also written Jhumar or Jhumur, is a folk song and dance form of eastern India, mainly the Chota Nagpur plateau. Wikipedia says the name comes from Jhum, a regional word for shifting cultivation, and that the songs began as short cries of women working in fields. Themes include love, riddles, social comment and, later, stories of Radha-Krishna.

Janani Jhumair is the women's form. Women hold hands in a line, sing and dance in a circle while men play the instruments. Mardani Jhumair is danced by men with ghungroo and swords. The common instruments are the mandar, dhol, bansi, nagara, dhak and shehnai.

Domkach is a wedding dance. Women and men from the groom's and the bride's families take part, forming a semicircle and holding each other's waists. Wikipedia lists three forms in Jharkhand: Ekharia, Dohri and Jhumta. The name is said to come from the dambru, an instrument.
artist: The music is community music. Wikipedia on Nagpuri culture says the instruments are traditionally made and played at marriages by the Ghasi and Mahli communities. The dance is held at the akhra, the village dance ground, which the page calls an important part of Nagpuri culture.

Jhumar is sung by agricultural and Indigenous communities such as Kurmi, Oraon, Munda and Bhumij. Mahavir Nayak is named on Wikipedia as a Theth Nagpuri singer, a genre built on folk ragas that draws on Jhumar. We found little else on named performers, so we name no others.
place: Nagpuri is the language of the Sadan community of the Chota Nagpur plateau, across central and western Jharkhand. Jhumar is also found in south-west West Bengal and northern Odisha, and among tea-garden communities in Assam.
The year is marked by the dances. Janani Jhumar begins in Ashadh (June to July) and runs to Kartik (October to November). The marriage season follows, with Domkach, until about Rath Yatra.

history.what: Wikipedia describes Jhumar as beginning with working women's songs in the fields, with religious themes added later. We found no firm dates.
Jhumar festivals include Karam and Jitiya. Domkach is danced in the marriage season.
Theth Nagpuri is a recorded genre based on Jhumar, Pawas, Udasi and Fagua ragas.

future: Support village akhra dances and make time for them at festivals.
Pay the Ghasi and Mahli instrument makers and players fairly, and teach young people to make mandar and dhol.
Record songs with the singers and note their words in Nagpuri and Kurmali.
Encourage women and men to teach children in schools in Jharkhand.
Document each local variant instead of treating Jhumair as one style.

name: Kalbelia
tagline: Women in swirling black skirts move like a snake, to the sound of the poongi.
facts: Form: song and dance of the Kalbelia community
Instruments: khanjari (percussion) and poongi (woodwind)
Oral tradition: no texts or training manuals
Inscribed by UNESCO in 2010
art: Kalbelia songs and dances belong to the Kalbelia community of Rajasthan. UNESCO describes them as once professional snake handlers, whose music and dance still recall that old occupation.

Women dance in flowing black skirts, swirling and bending in a way that imitates a serpent's movement. Men accompany them on the khanjari, a percussion instrument, and the poongi, a woodwind that was traditionally played to charm snakes. Wikipedia adds other instruments such as the dufli, been, morchang and dholak, and says the rhythm speeds up as the performance goes on.

Dancers wear traditional tattoo designs, jewellery, and richly embroidered clothes decorated with small mirrors and silver thread. Wikipedia names the angrakhi (upper cloth), odhani (headcloth) and lehenga, embroidered in red and black tones.

The songs pass on mythological stories, and the community is known for making up lyrics on the spot during a performance. Special dances are performed at Holi. All of this is handed down by ear and by watching: UNESCO notes that there are no texts or training manuals.
artist: The Kalbelia are also called Sapera, Jogira and Poogiwara in some sources. Wikipedia lists them as a Scheduled Tribe, divided into Daliwal and Mewara groups, who traditionally lived a travelling life in camps called deras. They follow the Nath tradition and revere Shiva and the cobra.

Snake catching was their traditional work. Wikipedia says the Wildlife Act of 1972 pushed them out of it, and that performing arts became a major but seasonal and tourism-dependent source of income. It also says the British listed them under the Criminal Tribes Act, which was repealed in 1952, and that stigma has lingered.
Wikipedia credits Dr. Gulabo Sapera with the Padma Shri for reviving the dance and taking it to a global audience. We have not found a fuller biography in the pages we read, so we say no more here.
place: The largest Kalbelia population is in Pali district, with groups in Ajmer, Chittorgarh and Udaipur districts, according to Wikipedia. These are the dry and hilly lands of southern and central Rajasthan.

UNESCO notes that the community's travelling way of life and its role in village society are fading, which makes song and dance an important marker of identity. Today the dance is seen at festivals, weddings and tourist events.

history.what: Wikipedia says the community looks back on the 12th and 13th centuries as a golden age. This comes from oral and secondary accounts and is hard to date.
Wikipedia says Kalbelia later performed at Mughal courts. We could not check this against a primary source.
The community was listed under the Criminal Tribes Act, according to Wikipedia.
The Act was repealed and the tribes were denotified.
The Wildlife Protection Act limited snake handling, and performance grew in importance as a livelihood, as Wikipedia describes it.
UNESCO inscribed Kalbelia folk songs and dances of Rajasthan on the Representative List of the Intangible Cultural Heritage of Humanity (decision 5.COM 6.16).

future: Support family and community teaching of the songs, so that improvised lyrics and older verses are not lost.
Build the Kalbelia cultural centre and archive that UNESCO's nomination describes, run with the community.
Pay performers fairly and year-round, not only in the tourist season.
Record songs with the singers' names, meanings and Marwari or local-language texts, with the community's consent.
Back schooling and other work options so that dance is a choice and not the only livelihood, and challenge the stigma that remains.

name: Karagattam
tagline: A decorated pot held on the head, and a dancer who must never let it fall.
facts: Form: folk dance with a pot balanced on the head
Two types: Sakthi Karagam (ritual) and Aattam Karagam (entertainment)
Linked to the goddess Mariamman
Performed by women and men
art: The name joins karagam, a water pot, and attam, dance. The dancer carries a pot on the head and moves, bends and turns without letting it fall. The pot may be of clay or metal, empty or full of water, and it is decorated, mostly with neem leaves and flowers. Wikipedia says some dancers stack several pots.
Wikipedia describes two kinds. Sakthi Karagam is performed only in temples as a spiritual offering. Aattam Karagam is done for entertainment and joy.
PARI says both men and women perform. Wikipedia says women traditionally wore saris, and that men in make-up sometimes joined as part of the story.
artist: I did not find a source naming the performers or troupes of Karagattam that I could verify. PARI's report by Aparna Karthikeyan covers performers in the Kanchipuram area, but the page I could read gave only a short summary.

Wikipedia notes that the dance has changed a good deal in this century. Some stage versions use revealing costumes and bright make-up, and it has gained a bad name in some places. It also cites a News Minute article on the art languishing under moral pressure. Performers deserve to be seen as skilled artists, not judged by that reputation.
Our approach: meet the performers in person, ask for their own account of training and income, and report it in their words.
place: Karagattam is a folk dance of Tamil Nadu, mostly rural. PARI's report on it is datelined Kanchipuram. Some accounts say it began in Thanjavur district, but sources differ, and I did not find a scholarly source for the origin.
It is performed at village festivals, at temples and in cultural programmes. Wikipedia links it to worship of the goddess Mariamman and to prayers for rain.
Wikipedia also records a Caribbean form, Karagam Puja, brought by indentured workers, and Singapore's heritage site lists karagam crafts and practices as intangible heritage.

history.what: Wikipedia says the dance is ancient and, according to Tamil literature, arose from a mix of Bharatham and other folk forms. Other websites claim a mention in Sangam literature, which I could not confirm.
Indentured workers took the tradition to the Caribbean, where it survives as Karagam Puja (Wikipedia).
Wikipedia notes significant change in costume and style on stage, and public debate about it.

future: Document the temple form (Sakthi Karagam) with the performers and temple communities, and keep their consent.
Offer training and fair pay to young performers, with respect for the ritual meaning.
Work with performers to set standards for costume and conduct that protect them, and let them decide how the art is shown.
Support the makers of the pots, flower garlands and music who make a performance possible.
Publish an open record of the forms, with video, in Tamil and English.

name: Karma and Rai Dances
tagline: A circle dance around a sacred branch in the east, and a swirling women's dance in Bundelkhand.
facts: Karma: tribal festival dance of central and eastern India
Karma: dancers circle a Karam branch, with a drum in the middle
Rai: dance of Bundelkhand, performed by Bedia women, per one source
Evidence on Rai in my sources is thin
art: Karma is a folk dance of central and eastern India, performed at the Karma festival. Wikipedia says dancers gather around a branch of the Karam tree, which is revered. The branch is passed between dancers and should not touch the ground. The festival honours Karam Devta, god of fate, and begins on the 11th day of the bright fortnight of Bhadrapada.
Dancers form a circle with arms around each other's waists. Men spring forward and women bend low, in a to-and-fro rhythm. A drum placed on the ground between the dancers sets the beat (Wikipedia).

Rai is a dance of Bundelkhand. One source says it is traditionally performed by women of the Bedia community in long lehengas, and takes its name from the swirling of mustard seeds. This is from one exam-preparation website; I could not corroborate it, so treat it with caution.
artist: Karma is a community dance, with no single named artist. The Gond and Baiga are the groups most often named in Madhya Pradesh. Another source says it is performed by Gond and Oraon communities in the rainy season, so accounts differ.

For Rai, the same source says Bedia women are the traditional performers. I could not find enough reliable sources to describe the community's own account or present situation, so this section is short.
place: Wikipedia lists Chhattisgarh, Jharkhand, Madhya Pradesh, Odisha and West Bengal as places where Karma is performed. In Madhya Pradesh the tradition is strongest in the eastern districts such as Mandla, Dindori and Balaghat, where the Gond and Baiga live.
Bundelkhand, where Rai is performed, spans parts of Uttar Pradesh and Madhya Pradesh.

history.what: I found no reliable source that dates either dance.
Karma is held on the 11th day of the bright fortnight of Bhadrapada, roughly August to September (Wikipedia).
Karma is still danced at festival time; I found no reliable page on its present state.

future: Training: festival and school programmes in which elders teach the songs and steps.
Livelihood: pay for community troupes at museums and festivals.
Materials: keep making drums, anklets and costumes locally.
Documentation: record Karma songs in Gondi and Baigani, and seek out Rai performers for their own account.
Protection: keep the festival itself, not only the stage version, alive in villages.

name: Kathak
tagline: The storyteller's dance of north India: fast footwork, whirling turns and a conversation with the drum.
facts: Form: solo dance with footwork, spins and story
Name comes from katha, meaning story
Main gharanas: Jaipur, Lucknow, Banaras
Recognised by Sangeet Natak Akademi as a classical dance
art: Kathak takes its name from the Sanskrit word katha, story. It is traditionally linked to wandering storytellers of north India, called kathakas or kathakars, who told stories from the epics and Puranas through speech, song and gesture.

A performance has two sides. In pure dance (nritta), the dancer plays with rhythm in cycles called tala. The footwork is called tatkar. Short pieces called tukra, tora and paran, and the long spoken rhythm syllables (bols), are built on it. In expressive dance (nritya and abhinaya), the dancer tells a poem or a story with the face and hands. Spins, called chakkar, are a mark of the style.
Kathak often includes a duet between dancer and tabla or pakhawaj player, each answering the other's phrases. The dancer's ankle bells, ghungroo, are part of the music.

Wikipedia notes that under the Mughal rulers the art moved from temples to palace courts and took in Persian and Central Asian influences such as costume and some forms of poetry. Kathak today carries both the Hindu devotional stories of Krishna and a courtly, Persian-influenced side.
artist: Kathak is taught through gharanas, families and schools of teaching. Wikipedia names three main ones. The Jaipur gharana is known for sharp footwork, rhythmic work and spins, and its origin is traced to Bhanuji, whose grandsons Laluji and Kanhuji are credited with founding it. The Lucknow gharana is known for grace and expression, and traced to Ishwari Prasad of Handia in Uttar Pradesh. The Banaras gharana is known for its footwork and Krishna stories, and Janakiprasad is credited with its bols. Wikipedia also describes a Raigarh style, from the court of Raja Chakradhar Singh.

Within Lucknow, the Kalka-Bindadin family is among the best-known lines of teachers. Pandit Birju Maharaj belonged to this line and taught for many years in Delhi. I could not confirm his dates or posts from a primary source, so we will source them before publication.
Training begins with posture, basic footwork and the tala system, then adds bols, compositions and expression. The relationship with a guru and with the musicians is central.
Our approach: record the family lines of gurus, musicians and tabla players, not only the soloist.
place: Kathak grew across the plains of north India, where the storytelling traditions of the temple and the village meeting place met the courts of Rajput princes and Mughal rulers. Jaipur in Rajasthan, Lucknow, once the capital of the Nawabs of Awadh, and Varanasi (Banaras) are the three main seats.

Wikipedia says the Awadh ruler Wajid Ali Shah (reigned 1847 to 1856) was himself a practitioner of the dance, and Lucknow's court culture is often linked with the gentle, expressive side of Kathak. Jaipur's courts are linked with the strong rhythmic side. Varanasi is a major centre of both music and Krishna devotion.
Today Delhi is a main centre. The Sangeet Natak Akademi runs Kathak Kendra there. I did not find an exact founding date in the sources I read, so I leave it out.

history.what: Kathakas, storytellers, are mentioned in old texts such as the Mahabharata, according to Wikipedia. How far they relate directly to today's Kathak is a matter of scholarly debate.
Bhakti poetry spreads Krishna stories across north India and storytellers carry them to temples and villages.
Kathak moves into courts and takes on Persian and Central Asian elements, according to Wikipedia.
Wajid Ali Shah of Awadh, himself a practitioner, supports dance and music at Lucknow.
The three gharanas, Jaipur, Lucknow and Banaras, take distinct shape. Dates of their founders are not agreed in the sources I read.
Teachers from the gharanas begin to teach in cities and institutions, and the dance moves from courts to public stages.
Sangeet Natak Akademi recognises Kathak among the classical dances of India. I could not confirm the exact year.
Kathak is taught across India and abroad, with new work that combines it with other dance forms.

future: Support the families of sarangi, tabla and pakhawaj players who accompany Kathak and are rarely named.
Record the compositions (bandish, tukra, paran) of each gharana with the elder gurus, with bol notation and video.
Offer scholarships for young dancers from small towns in Uttar Pradesh and Rajasthan, away from the big cities.
Preserve the storytelling side, such as thumri and bhav, with training in Hindi, Urdu and Braj poetry.
Collect oral histories of the court, temple and later women performers of Lucknow and Banaras, and share them in a public archive.
Build live music into classes and shows so that recorded tracks do not replace the musicians.

name: Kathakali
tagline: Gods and demons in green, red and black faces, told through the eyes and hands.
facts: Form: dance-drama with gesture, music and drums
Face types: pacha, kathi, kari, thadi, minukku
Stories: from the Ramayana, Mahabharata and Puranas
Traditionally dated to the 17th century
art: Kathakali is a dance-drama from Kerala. The actors do not speak. Singers on stage sing the story, drummers play the chenda and maddalam, and the actors tell it through gesture (mudra), eye movement and facial expression.

What most people remember first is the face. Characters are grouped by their make-up and costume, called vesham. Kerala Tourism lists five main types. Pacha has a green face for noble, heroic characters. Kathi is for proud or villainous heroes. Kari is black, for hunters and forest dwellers. Thadi means bearded: a red beard for the most wicked, white for refined characters such as Hanuman, black for lesser evil. Minukku has a yellowish face and is used for women, sages and messengers. Other writers count the categories differently.

The face painting is called theppu. The chutti is a raised white ridge along the jaw that frames the face. It was once made of rice paste and is now made of paper, and it can take hours to put on. The eyes are reddened with natural herbs so that small movements can be seen from a distance. The big skirts, jackets and crowns are together called koppu.

The plays are called attakatha. They are written in Malayalam-Sanskrit verse and draw on the epics and Puranas. Kerala Tourism notes that the Kottayam royal family wrote four major Mahabharata plays that became a base for the repertoire.

Traditionally a play was staged overnight, and some stories ran across several nights, starting with a drum call at dusk called kelikottu. Today performances are often a few hours long, on stage and in halls.
artist: A Kathakali actor trains for many years before a first stage appearance. Kerala Tourism says the training borrows body movement from Kalaripayattu and gesture and expression from Koodiyattam. Students rise very early, and Kalamandalam's own pages mention classes starting at 4.30 in the morning, with exercise and massage as part of the day.

The art is not only the actors. Singers, drummers, costume keepers and the make-up artists, known as chuttikkar, work together. Chutti is taught as its own skill: Kerala Tourism lists training in chutti at institutions such as PSV Natyasangham in Kottakkal and the Kathakali Sadanam in Ottapalam.
Historically only men performed, taking women's roles too. Kerala Tourism says women now perform at all levels.
Our approach: name the actors, singers and make-up artists in every story, and show the hours behind a single face.
place: Kathakali grew in the old kingdoms of Kerala, with the first form, Ramanattam, linked to Kottarakkara in the south and later development under patrons in Kottayam (Malabar) and the Cochin region. Temple courtyards and royal houses were its first stages.

Today the main training centres are spread across the state. Kerala Kalamandalam is at Cheruthuruthy on the Bharathapuzha river, near Shoranur. Other places include Kottakkal (PSV Natyasangham, run under Arya Vaidya Sala), Ottapalam, Thiruvananthapuram (the Margi centre, started in 1974 on the gurukula model) and Kochi, where regular shows are staged for visitors.

Kerala's wet, green landscape and its temple festival calendar shape when and where Kathakali is seen. The festival season is the heart of its livelihood, and it is also now a major draw for cultural tourism.

history.what: Older temple arts such as Koodiyattam and Krishnanattam are named by scholars as sources of Kathakali's gesture, make-up and stage style.

Kerala Tourism says the form is believed to have evolved in this century. A king of Kottarakkara is credited with Ramanattam, the Ramayana drama that came before Kathakali. A popular story says he made it after the Zamorin refused to lend him a Krishnanattam troupe. Historians treat this as legend and sources differ on details.
The Kottayam royal family wrote four major Mahabharata plays that became the base of the repertoire.
Kaplingad Narayanan Namboodiri is credited with refining the art, giving rise to the Kaplingadan style.
The poet Vallathol Narayana Menon and Mukunda Raja formed Kerala Kalamandalam. Wikipedia gives 1927 for the society and November 1930 for its inauguration at Kunnamkulam; Kerala Tourism gives 1930.
Kalamandalam settled at Cheruthuruthy on land and a building given by the Maharaja of Cochin. Some sources give 1933, so the year is uncertain.
Pattikkamthodi Ravunni Menon is credited with setting down the scattered systems, leading to the Kalluvazhi style.
The Margi centre in Thiruvananthapuram began Kathakali training in the gurukula way.
Kalamandalam was granted deemed-university status.

future: Fund full-time gurukula places for children from families of drummers, singers and make-up artists, who are often forgotten.
Give chuttikkar and costume makers recognised training and fair pay, not only the actors.
Record whole attakatha performances with the senior gurus, with Malayalam and English notes, and keep them in an open archive.
Run small-town and village performances in the festival off-season, so artists have year-round work.
Source natural dyes, rice and bamboo costume materials in ways that are fair to the farmers and craft families who supply them.
Offer visitors a proper introduction before shows: the story, the face types, and a chance to meet the artists.

name: Khuallam
tagline: The dance of the guests, once part of the great feast that earned a man the Thangchhuah title.
facts: Name: khual (guest) plus lam (dance)
Music: gongs and drum, no songs
Dress: puandum for women, ngotekherh for men (Wikipedia)
