Once linked to the Khuangchawi feast
art: Khuallam means dance of the guests. Wikipedia says dancers sway large shawls and are accompanied by a dar (gong) and khuang (drum), usually in 7/8 time. No songs are sung. IGNCA names the gongs as darbu.

Wikipedia describes the steps. Dancers extend one arm while stepping forward, then pull the arm back so that the shawl sways, and repeat on the other side. In the second part a man and woman face each other, sway and bend, and push their elbows back to move the cloth.

The dress is a handwoven black shawl striped red, yellow and green, called puandum, for women, and a large white shawl with black patterns, called ngotekherh, for men, according to Wikipedia. IGNCA says men wear puandum in this dance. The sources do not agree.
It is still performed for honoured visitors. Festival shows may add steps such as lifting the cloth high and squatting.
artist: Khuallam belongs to the Mizo community and has no named master. I found no named performers or teachers.

A journal source found in search says it was traditionally danced by men and that women now often dance alongside them in cultural programmes. I could not read the PDF to check, so treat this as unconfirmed.
place: Mizoram is a hill state in north-east India. The dance belongs to the older Mizo feast tradition, before Christianity became the main religion.
Today it is part of festivals such as Chapchar Kut and is shown at state functions. A search result says it has been revived since the 1970s; I could not confirm that.

history.what: Wikipedia and IGNCA say Khuallam was performed at the Khuangchawi, the last rite on the road to the Thangchhuah title, when invited guests danced on their way to the feast. IGNCA calls it the seventh and final rite.
Wikipedia says the Mizo believed the title, earned through feasts or hunting, was needed to enter Pialral, the heaven. Accounts of the requirements vary.

Wikipedia gives a legend that friends of Tlatea's third son carried wine pots wrapped in a large cloth into Kawilam during Chapchar Kut, and townspeople took the moving cloth for dancing guests. Treat it as a story.
Wikipedia says it is now part of major Mizo cultural festivals.

future: Training: teach the steps and the meaning in schools and youth clubs, with elders.
Livelihood: pay performers for festival and guest-welcome shows.
Materials: keep weaving of puandum and ngotekherh alive for costumes.
Documentation: film performances and record the Thangchhuah story with elders, including where accounts differ.
Protection: involve cultural bodies in listing and recording the dance.

name: Kolkali
tagline: Pairs of men strike short sticks in a widening circle, faster and faster.
facts: Name: kol means stick
Men dance in pairs in a circle
Kerala Tourism: about 200 years old, from North Malabar
Called one of the two popular folk arts of Lakshadweep
art: Kolkali is a stick dance. Dancers hold short sticks, move in a circle and strike the sticks together in time with the music. Kerala Tourism says the circle expands and contracts, the dancers do not touch one another or miss a beat, and near the end the steps become vigorous with sweeping turns.
The music rises in pitch and the pace quickens until the peak. Maps of India says that on Lakshadweep the dance starts slowly and speeds up, with folk songs, and that only men perform it.
The dance is said to have drawn on Kalaripayattu, the martial art of Kerala. Kerala Tourism says the same, while Wikipedia says it borrowed training methods, postures and footwork from it.
Related stick dances are Kolattam in Tamil Nadu and Kolamu in Andhra Pradesh, according to Kerala Tourism.
artist: In Kerala, Wikipedia says Kolkali is a folk art of the Malabar region, performed by Hindu and Muslim groups, and that some older styles, such as Thacholikali, are almost extinct, while a southern style, Thekkan Koladi, survives in school youth festivals. That article is flagged as weakly sourced.
In Lakshadweep, I found no named teachers or troupes. The administration names Kolkali as one of the two popular folk arts.
place: Kolkali is shared between two places. In Kerala it belongs to North Malabar, the northern coast of the state. Lakshadweep lies in the Arabian Sea off that same coast, and the two have long contact.
On Lakshadweep, the administration says Kolkali and Parichakali are the popular folk arts of the islands, except Minicoy where Lava is preferred.

history.what: Kerala Tourism says Kolkali has about 200 years of history. Some educational sites claim over a thousand years, but I found no good source for that.
Sources link the dance to Kalaripayattu, though the exact path is not documented.
Kerala Tourism says the dance has influenced folk dances in Bengal, Gujarat, Punjab and Maharashtra. I treat this as that source's view.
The administration calls Kolkali one of the popular folk arts of the islands. I found no account of when it arrived.

future: Record the older Kerala styles that are close to disappearing, with the senior players.
Find and document the Lakshadweep songs and steps and see how they differ from the Malabar ones.
Support the competitions and youth festivals that keep young dancers training.
Make sticks locally and sustainably, with makers paid for them.
Write the shared history of Kolkali jointly with performers from Malabar and the islands.

name: Kuchipudi
tagline: A dance-drama from a single village, once played by Brahmin men and now danced by many.
facts: Named for Kuchipudi village in Krishna district
Traditionally credited to Siddhendra Yogi
Sung in Telugu to Carnatic music
Troupes were all male; women now dominate
art: Kuchipudi is a dance-drama from Andhra Pradesh. It joins nritta (pure dance), nritya (expression with gesture) and natya (drama). The language of the songs is Telugu, and the music is Carnatic, with mridangam, violin, flute, cymbals and tambura.
Wikipedia notes that the dance is rooted in the Natya Shastra and in older Telugu performing traditions. Its stories are devotional, drawn from the Bhagavata Purana and the Krishna tradition.

A famous piece is the Bhama Kalapam, the story of Satyabhama, a wife of Krishna, tradition says composed by Siddhendra Yogi. Kuchipudi also has playful, physical items. Wikipedia mentions kavutvams, which are acrobatic feats such as dancing while balancing pots.
Expression and speech are important. Dancers traditionally spoke or sang lines, which makes Kuchipudi closer to theatre than some other classical dances.
artist: According to tradition, as Wikipedia reports, Siddhendra Yogi, a disciple of the sanyasin Tirtha Narayana Yati, shaped the modern form in the 17th century. His play Parijatapaharana, now called Bhama Kalapam, was performed by young Brahmin boys of Kuchipudi (Kuchelapuram), and the villagers agreed to stage it each year. Some traditions credit another figure, Narahari Tirtha, so this is not settled.

For centuries the performers were Brahmin men of Kuchipudi families, who took women's roles too. Their troupes, called melas, travelled to temples and courts. Wikipedia reports that after the fall of the Vijayanagara empire (about 1565) many families moved, and in 1678 the Golconda ruler Abul Hasan Tana Shah gave land to the artists.

In the 20th century the art was revived and moved to solo performance. Wikipedia credits Vedantam Lakshminarayana Sastri with leading this work from the 1920s to the 1950s, with Vempati Venkatanarayana Sastri and Chinta Venkataramayya among others. After the 1958 All India Dance Seminar, the dance reached national attention. Vempati Chinna Satyam (Padma Bhushan) is credited with codifying the modern repertoire and teaching in Chennai.
Women now form most of the performers, and solo and duet shows are common.
place: Kuchipudi village lies in Krishna district, near the delta of the Krishna river in coastal Andhra Pradesh. The region has been a crossing of Telugu kingdoms, from the Vijayanagara period to the Golconda sultanate.

The village is associated with the temple of Bala Tripura Sundari and with Brahmin families who held the performing tradition as a hereditary duty. The village is still a centre of training, and a school for dance (Siddhendra Kalakshetram) stands there.
Chennai (Madras) is also part of the story, as many Kuchipudi families and gurus moved there in the 20th century, which led to the form's wider reach.

history.what: Copper inscriptions of the 10th century and the 15th-century Machupalli Kaifat mention older forms of Telugu dance-drama, according to Wikipedia.
Siddhendra Yogi is credited with systematising the modern form. Some traditions name another founder.
The Vijayanagara empire falls, and many artist families move away, according to Wikipedia.
The Golconda ruler Abul Hasan Tana Shah grants land to the dancers, according to Wikipedia.
Campaigns against temple and court dancing and the 1910 Madras Presidency ban add to the decline of the art.
Vedantam Lakshminarayana Sastri and others lead a revival, and women begin to learn the dance.
The All India Dance Seminar brings Kuchipudi to national attention.
Vempati Chinna Satyam codifies the modern repertoire and trains many students.

future: Support the surviving Kuchipudi village families who still hold the dance-drama, and keep a regular yearly performance in the village.
Record full-length dance-dramas such as the Bhama Kalapam, with the spoken parts in Telugu, to keep the theatre side alive.
Open training to students from all communities, with scholarships for children from villages in Andhra and Telangana.
Teach male dancers and women's roles by men, so the older tradition is also kept in the classroom.
Pay musicians, singers and costume makers fairly for stage work.
Build a small museum and archive in Kuchipudi village for manuscripts, photographs and costumes.

name: Kullu Nati
tagline: A slow-then-quickening circle dance of the Kullu valley, danced by thousands at Dussehra.
facts: Form: circle folk dance, to drums and horns
Occasions: births, weddings, harvests, Dussehra, Diwali
Guinness record: 9,892 dancers, 26 October 2015, Kullu
Setting: Kullu Dussehra, begins on Vijay Dashmi, lasts seven days
art: Nati is a folk dance of the western and central hills, mainly in Himachal Pradesh. It has many forms: Kullvi, Mahasuvi, Sirmauri, Kinnauri, Jaunpuri and others. Kullu Nati is the form of the Kullu valley.

Dancers form circles or semicircles and move forward and back. Partners may hold hands in a criss-cross pattern, or dance with hands swaying. Footwork varies by place but shares a basic set of eight steps. The tempo starts slow and quickens with the music.

Music comes from the dhol, karnal, narsingha, shehnai and nagara. Musicians are called tunis. Dancers wear the Himachali cap, woollen clothes, the Kullu pattu or sadri jackets, and the dhattu head scarf for women.
Nati is danced at births, weddings, harvests and festivals. After a sacred performance, a yagna is held to honour the deities.
artist: Any number of people can take part. Wikipedia says men performed Nati in the past, but women now mostly carry the tradition. Male leaders often carry a fly whisk or an axe.
I did not find sourced names of individual Kullu Nati masters, so none are listed here.

In 2015 the District Administration of Kullu organised a mass Nati, listed by Guinness as the largest Nati dance with 9,892 participants. Wikipedia says the dancers were women, and a news report says the dance carried a message to save the girl child.
place: Kullu valley lies along the Beas in the Himalaya. The Dussehra festival is held at the Dhalpur Maidan in Kullu town and is given international festival status by the state. It draws several hundred thousand people.

Local legend says Raja Jagat Singh installed the idol of Raghunath from Ayodhya and became the god's regent, and the festival is said to have started in 1606. It is a legend, and the date is traditional.

history.what: Kullu Dussehra is said to begin when Raghunath is installed in the valley.
A mass folk dance of 8,540 artists at Dussehra enters the Limca Book of Records (news report).
9,892 dancers perform Nati at Kullu Dussehra.
Guinness confirmation is announced.

future: Training: teach Nati steps and songs in village schools and cultural societies.
Livelihood: pay fees to local musicians and dancers who perform at festivals.
Materials: support makers of dhol, karnal and narsingha, and of costumes such as the pattu.
Documentation: record regional Nati variants and their songs on video and audio.
Protection: keep village performances alive alongside the festival stage.

name: Lavani
tagline: Quick, rhythmic song and dance to the dholki, in a nine-yard saree.
facts: Song-and-dance form accompanied by the dholki
Two main kinds: nirguni (devotional) and shringari (romantic)
Central to Tamasha, Maharashtra's folk theatre
Dancers wear the nauvari, a nine-yard saree
art: Lavani is a Maharashtrian form of song and dance, usually accompanied by the dholki, a two-headed hand drum. It is quick and rhythmic, and it has shaped Marathi folk theatre. Wikipedia describes two main types of song: nirguni, which is devotional and philosophical, and shringari, which is romantic.
In performance there are two settings. Phadachi lavani is staged before a large audience and is a central part of a Tamasha troupe's show. Baithakichi lavani is sung seated, in a private gathering.

The dancer wears a nauvari, a nine-yard saree draped in a trouser-like style, with heavy jewellery, a bun and a large bindi. The singing is answered by the chorus, and the dancer uses her eyes, hands and footwork to act the song.

The songs are in Marathi and range from love and humour to social comment and devotion. Poets named in accounts of lavani include Honaji Bala, Ram Joshi, Parasharam and, in the twentieth century, Annabhau Sathe. Wikipedia credits Honaji Bala with developing the baithakichi style.
artist: Women are the lead performers in lavani. Scholars note that many come from communities such as the Kolhati, Mahar and Matang, and that in baithakichi lavani the dancers were mainly Kolhati women, for whom dance was a caste-based profession.

These women are often the main earners in their families. Scholar Lata Singh writes that performers see the stage as a livelihood that has earned them professional respect. She also writes that the same women face stigma, and that lavani is wrongly equated with prostitution. A performer quoted by Open magazine recalls that Bombay banned lavani and Tamasha shows in 1948. I could not confirm the order itself from an official source.

Alongside the dancers are the drummers (dholki and tabla), the singers, the harmonium and tuntune players, and the poets. Men who dance beside the women have been called nat or kinnar in some accounts.

Names often given to well-known performers include Vithabai Narayangaonkar, Surekha Punekar and Yamunabai Waikar. I have not verified their honours, so none are stated. Our approach: speak with performers and their families, let them tell their own stories, and keep their dignity at the centre.
place: Lavani belongs to the western Deccan, mostly Maharashtra's Pune and Satara regions and the nearby Tamasha circuit. Narayangaon, north of Pune, is the home town named in the surname of the performer Vithabai Narayangaonkar. Tamasha troupes tour villages, though I did not find a source for the exact fair-season pattern.

The dance grew in a land of forts, courts and pilgrim fairs. Under the Maratha and later Peshwa rulers, as Wikipedia describes, court and private gatherings gave lavani patrons. After that it moved to open-air stages and into the tent shows of Tamasha.
Mumbai and Pune now have theatres and film connections for lavani. Marathi films such as Pinjara and Natarang brought it to a wider audience, according to Wikipedia.

history.what: Some writers link lavani songs to old Prakrit verse, but the link is debated. Wikipedia says its beginnings may go back to the 16th century.
Lavani was patronised by the Maratha rulers and flourished under the Peshwas. Poet-singers such as Honaji Bala and Ram Joshi are named in this period.
Lavani became a core part of Tamasha, the folk theatre of Maharashtra.
A performer quoted in Open magazine says lavani and Tamasha shows were banned in Bombay as indecent. The details need checking against official records.
Poets such as Annabhau Sathe wrote for the stage, and Marathi films carried lavani to wider audiences.
Bin Baykancha Tamasha, a show performed only by men, was started, according to the sources I read, to question the idea that women entertain male audiences. This claim needs checking.
Lavani is performed at jatras, on city stages, on television and in films. Performers continue to seek better pay and social respect.

future: Give lavani artists health cover, old-age support and fair contracts, since income is irregular and often depends on a single season.
Fund schooling and scholarships for the children of Tamasha families, so that the next generation has choices.
Record the songs, poets and music of lavani with the performers' consent, and credit them by name.
Offer training spaces for young dancers, with senior performers as paid teachers.
Present lavani in schools and festivals as a skilled art, with the performers' own voices.
Work with communities and scholars to challenge the stigma attached to the art and its performers.

name: Manipuri Dance
tagline: A soft, flowing dance of Radha and Krishna, from the hills and valley of Manipur.
facts: Form: devotional dance of the Meitei people
Roots: Lai Haraoba, Ras Lila and Sankirtana
Barrel-shaped kumin skirt for women
Sankirtana of Manipur on UNESCO list in 2013
art: Manipuri dance is the classical dance of Manipur. Its movements are gentle and rounded, with soft steps and mostly peaceful expression. Wikipedia describes it as made up of four ritual traditions: Lai Haraoba, Huyen Langlon (a martial art), Meitei Nata Sankirtana and Raaslila.

Its main stories are the love of Radha and Krishna, shown in the Ras Lila dances. Women wear the potloi, a stiff, decorated barrel-shaped skirt (also called kumin) with a veil, and men wear a dhoti and headdress.

Music comes from the pung (a barrel drum), kartal cymbals and singers, with flute and other instruments added. The Meitei Nata Sankirtana, singing and dancing in worship, was inscribed by UNESCO on its Representative List of the Intangible Cultural Heritage of Humanity in 2013. UNESCO describes a typical performance as two drummers and about ten singer-dancers surrounded by seated devotees.
The pung cholom, a drum dance, and the jagoi, the form of dance in the Manipur tradition, are part of the wider family. I could not verify more detail on them in the sources read.
artist: Dancers in Manipur learn within temple and community settings, from teachers called gurus, and from the mentor-to-pupil handing down that UNESCO describes for Sankirtana. Women dancers and male drummers, the pung players, have different roles.

The older Lai Haraoba is a festival for the pre-Vaishnava Meitei deities (the Umang Lai), where priests and priestesses (maibas and maibis) take a key part in the ritual and dance. The Vaishnava forms grew on top of this.

In 1919 onward, Wikipedia says, Rabindranath Tagore helped bring Manipuri dance to Shantiniketan, which carried it to a wider Indian audience. The Sangeet Natak Akademi lists Manipuri among its classical dances.
Other names of the 20th century, such as the Jhaveri sisters and Manipuri gurus, appear in other accounts that I did not check in time.
place: Manipur is in north-east India, with a central valley ringed by hills. Imphal is in the valley, and the Meitei people live mostly there. The Shree Govindajee temple in Imphal is a main temple of the Vaishnava tradition, and Wikipedia says the dance survived mainly in temples after British annexation in 1891.

Loktak Lake and the rice fields of the valley frame the Lai Haraoba festival, which honours the old deities with songs and dance. Vaishnavism arrived in the plains over several centuries; sources differ, with one text giving the 15th century and another naming King Pitambar Charairongba in 1704.
The valley's culture is close to textile work too: the potloi and the dress are part of the craft world, which includes Manipuri weaving.

history.what: Lai Haraoba, a ritual for the old deities of the Meitei people, forms the oldest base of the dance. Dates are not agreed.
Vaishnavism enters Meitei life. Wikipedia gives two views: the 15th century, from the text Bamon Khunthok, and 1704, under King Pitambar Charairongba.
King Bhagyachandra (Rajarshi Bhagyachandra) is credited with shaping the classical Ras Lila form, according to Wikipedia.
Britain annexes Manipur, and the dance survives mainly in temples such as Shree Govindajee.
Rabindranath Tagore helps bring Manipuri dance to Shantiniketan, according to Wikipedia.
Sangeet Natak Akademi recognises Manipuri as a classical dance. I could not confirm the year.
UNESCO inscribes the Sankirtana of Manipur on the Representative List of the Intangible Cultural Heritage of Humanity.

future: Support the pung players, singers and temple teachers who hold Sankirtana, with fair stipends and apprentices.
Document Lai Haraoba, Ras Lila and pung cholom with the maibis, maibas and gurus, using Meiteilon and translation.
Open training to children across the valley and the hills, with scholarships.
Support the weavers and costume makers of the potloi and the kumin skirt.
Keep the art safe during periods of unrest by backing local teachers and performance spaces.
Build a public archive of drum syllables, songs and dance notation, held with the community.

name: Mohiniyattam
tagline: A slow, swaying dance in a white and gold sari, danced mostly by women.
facts: Form: solo classical dance of Kerala
Costume: white sari with gold kasavu border
Music: Carnatic style, lyrics in Manipravalam
One of eight classical dances recognised in India
art: Mohiniyattam is a solo classical dance of Kerala, danced by women. Its movement is soft and flowing, with swaying hips, a straight back and a side-to-side rhythm. Kerala Tourism says there are about 40 basic movements, called adavukal.

Hand gestures follow a treatise called Hastha Lakshanadeepika. The songs are in Manipravalam, a mix of Sanskrit and Malayalam. Themes are mostly devotion to Vishnu and Krishna and the love stories of the epics.

The costume is simple. It is an off-white sari with a broad gold border, called kasavu, the same cloth that is worn in Kerala at festivals such as Onam. A book by the dancer Kalamandalam Sathyabhama says the modern costume was shaped at Kerala Kalamandalam.
The repertoire, as sources describe, includes chollukettu, jatiswaram, varnam, padam and tillana, in a pattern that is close to Bharatanatyam.
artist: Women have been the dancers, teachers and in the modern period the reformers of Mohiniyattam. Kerala Tourism names the dancer and teacher Kalamandalam Kalyanikutty Amma as helping to restore the dance, and Kalamandalam Sathyabhama is also described as having shaped the Kalamandalam style.
Training today takes place at Kerala Kalamandalam and in private schools and academies in Kerala and abroad. Students learn music, rhythm syllables and expression alongside the steps.
Our approach: tell the story through the teachers' voices, and ask them how they would describe the dance in their own words.
place: Mohiniyattam is linked in most accounts to the Travancore kingdom in the south, with the court of Swathi Thirunal in Thiruvananthapuram. The Cochin region and Kerala Kalamandalam at Cheruthuruthy became the centre of the 20th century revival.
The kasavu cloth of the costume is also worn at Kerala festivals, which ties the dance to the state's handloom tradition.
Hot, humid weather shapes the light cotton, and temple festivals and cultural programmes give the dance its stages.

history.what: Scholars do not agree. One view sees roots in the lasya style of dance long known in Kerala. Kerala Tourism says temple dancers performed it under the Chera kings (9th to 12th century), but this is hard to prove.
The Balaramabharatam, a treatise attributed to Karthika Thirunal Balarama Varma of Travancore (1758-1798), is described as an early codification of Kerala's lasya tradition.

The Travancore king Swathi Thirunal is credited with steadying the dance with help from the Tanjore Quartet. Vadivelu, one of the Tanjore brothers, is linked with structuring the repertoire. Sources differ on how much each person did.
The dance fell out of favour and lost standing in society.
The poet Vallathol Narayana Menon founded Kerala Kalamandalam, which took up Mohiniyattam.
Kalamandalam Kalyanikutty Amma and Kalamandalam Sathyabhama helped shape and teach the modern form.
Kerala Kalamandalam became a deemed university.
The dance is taught widely in India and abroad and is recognised as a classical form.

future: Fund full scholarships at Kalamandalam and partner schools for girls and boys from rural and low-income families.
Support women teachers to open small neighbourhood classes and earn a living from teaching.
Publish the old Malayalam padams and the Balaramabharatam with translations, and record them with senior dancers.
Help handloom weavers of kasavu cloth earn a fair price through cooperatives, so the costume supports Kerala's weavers too.
Document the debate about the dance's origins openly, so students know what is known and what is not.
Create paid stage opportunities in schools and temples beyond the festival season.

name: Naga Festival Dances and Songs
tagline: Seventeen tribes' songs, dances and war cries on one stage at the Hornbill Festival.
facts: Hornbill Festival: 1 to 10 December each year, first held in December 2000
Venue: Kisama Heritage Village, about 12 km from Kohima
Run by the Government of Nagaland
Called the Festival of Festivals
art: Naga troupes perform folk songs and dances at the Hornbill Festival. Songs and dances are rooted in each tribe's own lore. Reports mention songs of love, war and harvest, and dances that praise warriors.

An Eastern Mirror report on the last day lists 17 troupes: Angami, Khiamniungan, Zeliang, Kachari, Yimchunger, Pochury, Sumi, Lotha, Chang, Sangtam, Konyak, Phom, Kuki, Ao, Rengma, Chakhesang and Garo. They performed from 10 am to 3 pm in two sessions.

The same report describes Chakhesang youths performing Uwhe, a war cry showing the martial training of boys. Young boys wrestled to show their training was done. Sumi men took part in an indigenous tug of war. Performers wore traditional dress in the cold.
A tourism article names a Chang song, He Lo He, performed to a log drum. I did not open that article, so I leave it as a pointer only.
artist: The performers are community troupes, often young people. Each tribe sends its own troupe in its own dress. The report quotes an Art and Culture department official saying that the troupes meet as strangers and leave as friends.
Tourism Deputy Director Veyielo Doulo is quoted saying that organising such a large event always brings criticism, but the department accepts it as a strength. The report gives this as his statement.
I did not find named song-keepers or choreographers in the sources I read.
place: Kisama Heritage Village lies in the southern Angami region of Kohima district, about 12 km from Kohima, per Wikipedia. The festival is organised by the Department of State Tourism and the Department of Art and Culture.
Wikipedia says it represents all of Nagaland's ethnic groups. Sources differ on how many tribes take part each year, with figures of 16 and 17 given in press reports.

history.what: The first Hornbill Festival is held, per Wikipedia.
Held from 1 to 10 December at Kisama. The government organises it to bring the state's tribes and culture together.
The Eastern Mirror report describes 17 cultural troupes performing in a recent edition.
Sources differ on tribe counts; Nagaland recognises many tribes and not all take part each year.

future: Training: tribal councils and schools could teach the songs through the year, not just before the festival.
Livelihood: the festival brings tourists and work for performers and craft sellers. Fair pay for troupes helps.
Materials: costumes use feathers, beads and woven cloth, which links to the shawl and beadwork crafts.
Documentation: audio and video of each tribe's songs, with lyrics and meanings, would help keep them.
Protection: staged performances should stay linked to the village festivals the songs came from.

name: Odissi
tagline: A dance of curves, in which the body bends into three, like the sculptures of Odisha's temples.
facts: Form: classical dance of Odisha, linked to Jagannath worship
Signature pose: tribhanga, the body bent in three
Old temple dancers: maharis and boy dancers called gotipuas
Revived in the mid 20th century
art: Odissi is the classical dance of Odisha. Its most striking mark is the tribhanga, a pose in which the head, chest and hips are shifted in three opposing curves. The chauka, a square, wide-knee stance, is the other basic position. Wikipedia lists 63 hand gestures in modern Odissi.

A typical recital, according to Wikipedia, moves through mangalacharana (an invocation), batu (pure dance), pallavi (flowing pure dance to a raga), nritya (expressive dance), natya (a short drama) and moksha (the closing). The poetry of Jayadeva's Gita Govinda, a 12th-century Sanskrit poem on Radha and Krishna, is central to its expressive pieces.

Many dance historians point to the sculpture of Odisha as a record of the dance. Wikipedia notes a cave at Udayagiri with carvings, the Hathigumpha inscription linked to King Kharavela that mentions dance and music, and temple sculpture at Konark, Bhubaneswar and Puri dated to between the 10th and 14th centuries. The link between these images and the dance of today is argued from sculpture and texts, and scholars disagree on how direct it is.
Music is Odissi music, sung in Odia and Sanskrit, with the pakhawaj or mardala drum, flute, sitar and cymbals.
artist: Two groups carried the dance before the 20th century. The maharis were women attached to temples, notably the Jagannath temple at Puri. The gotipuas were boys dressed as girls who danced in groups, often with acrobatic movement, and were attached to akharas, local training houses, and to temple festivals. Wikipedia describes both.

The anti-dance movement, which Wikipedia dates from 1892, and the 1910 ban on temple dancing in the Madras Presidency, made life hard for hereditary dancers in this period. The mahari tradition declined.

Guru Kelucharan Mohapatra (1926 to 2004), born at Raghurajpur near Puri, is credited by Wikipedia with a leading part in the revival of Odissi in the 20th century. His study of the gotipua and mahari dance shaped the form. He taught dancers such as Sanjukta Panigrahi and Sonal Mansingh. He received the Padma Vibhushan in 2000. With his wife Laxmipriya and son Ratikant he built the institution Srjan in 1993.

Wikipedia credits the poet Kalicharan Pattanayak with giving the dance its name Odissi in the 1950s. Other gurus of the revival, such as Pankaj Charan Das, Deba Prasad Das and Mayadhar Raut, are named in other accounts, which I did not check in time.
place: Odisha sits on the Bay of Bengal. Its three temple towns, Puri, Bhubaneswar and Konark, hold the Jagannath temple, the many temples of the old Kalinga style, and the Sun temple at Konark, whose walls carry musicians and dancers in stone.

Puri's Jagannath temple was the home of the maharis, who sang and danced in the daily service of the deity. The Gita Govinda is sung there as part of that service. Raghurajpur village, near Puri, is also known for its craftspeople and as the birthplace of Guru Kelucharan Mohapatra.
Bhubaneswar, the state capital, is now the main centre of teaching, with schools such as Srjan. Udayagiri and Khandagiri, caves near Bhubaneswar, are the earliest sites in the dance's story.

history.what: Carvings in the caves at Udayagiri, and the Hathigumpha inscription linked to King Kharavela, mention dance and music. Dates and readings are debated.
Temple sculpture at Bhubaneswar, Puri and Konark shows dancers and musicians.
Jayadeva writes the Gita Govinda, which becomes central to Odissi's expressive repertoire.
An anti-dance campaign begins in 1892 and temple dancing is banned in the Madras Presidency in 1910, according to Wikipedia. The effect on Odisha's maharis is described in other sources too.
Kalicharan Pattanayak is credited with naming the dance Odissi, and revival work grows after independence.
Guru Kelucharan Mohapatra lives and teaches. He is credited with reshaping Odissi in the 20th century.
Srjan is established at Bhubaneswar by Kelucharan Mohapatra, his wife and his son.
Kelucharan Mohapatra receives the Padma Vibhushan, the first recipient from Odisha, according to Wikipedia.

future: Document the surviving songs and memories of the last mahari dancers and gotipua gurus with their own words, in Odia, before they are lost.
Support gotipua akharas around Puri, such as in Raghurajpur, so boys and families who still train can make a living.
Connect Odissi training with the sculpture sites, so students and visitors can learn from Konark and Udayagiri on location.
Fund pakhawaj and mardala players, singers and costume and silver-jewellery makers with fair pay.
Build a public archive of Gita Govinda singing and Odissi music in the temple tradition.
Offer free community classes in Odisha's smaller towns.

name: Padayani
tagline: Giant painted masks, fire torches and the goddess Bhadrakali in the temples of central Travancore.
facts: Ritual art of Bhadrakali temples in central Travancore
Kolams: huge masked figures of areca spathe and palm leaf
Kadammanitta: a ten-day festival in Medam
Earliest cited mention: Talakkad inscription, 1024 CE
art: Padayani is a ritual art of Bhadrakali temples in central Kerala. Its main attraction is a theatrical procession of kolams. Performers wear heavy headgear, strong makeup and bold costumes and dance in whirling movements.

Kerala Tourism says the giant kolams at Kadammanitta are made of areca spathes and carefully cut palm leaves, lit by torches of dried coconut leaves. The kolams include Ganapathi, Marutha, Kalan, Kuthira, Madan, Pakshi, Yakshi and Bhairavi. The Bhairavi kolams are described as resembling the armies of Bhadrakali.

Drums are the thappu and chenda, and songs accompany the dance. The programme includes kolam songs, kolam thullal and a comic segment called vinodam. Paradeshi is the main comic interlude, per Kerala Tourism.
At Neelamperoor, the processions feature large swan figures made from flowers, lotus leaves and plantain stems.
artist: Wikipedia says Nair folk performed the dance while Kaniyar (Ganaka) people wrote the lyrics and made the costumes. Another account links padayani to a healing ritual of the Ganaka community. Another ties it to Kalari parades. The origin is not settled.

Wikipedia names Prof. Kadammanitta Vasudevan Pillai as a chief exponent and the poet Kadammanitta Ramakrishnan, who proposed a padayani village. It also credits T. K. Vasudevan Pilla Asan with reviving the Kunnamthanam padayani.
I did not find enough in the sources I could read to describe individual mask-makers.
place: Padayani belongs to central Travancore: Pathanamthitta and Kottayam districts and nearby parts of Kollam and Alappuzha. Festival sites include Kadammanitta, Kottangal, Othera, Kunnamthanam and Neelamperoor.

At Kadammanitta Bhagavathy Temple the festival opens with chootu vaipu, the lighting of fire from the temple lamp. The main day, Valiya Padayani, is the seventh. It ends with vallappattu boat songs, per Kerala Tourism.

history.what: The Talakkad inscription is the earliest cited mention, per Wikipedia.
Padayani is said to commemorate the dance that calmed Kali after she slew the demon Darika.
Wikipedia lists local revivals, such as Kunnamthanam.
Kadammanitta draws large festival crowds each Medam.

future: Train young kolam makers, since each kolam needs hours of skilled work.
Protect the areca and palm leaf supply and use only safe fire torches.
Document songs, rhythms and kolam designs with Ganaka and Nair families.
Pay performers and makers fairly, beyond festival season.
Support the proposed padayani village and a study centre.

name: Perini Shivatandavam
tagline: A fierce dance for Shiva, once done by warriors, read back from a medieval text and temple stone.
facts: Form: vigorous Tandava dance, mostly male
Text: Nritta Ratnavali by Jayapa Senani
Sculpture: Ramappa temple near Warangal
Revived by Dr Nataraja Ramakrishna (1923-2011)
art: Perini Shivatandavam is a dance for Shiva. It is vigorous, in the Tandava style, with a heroic mood (veera rasa). Wikipedia says dancers reached a trance-like state, inviting Shiva to dance through them.

Narthaki writes that Jayapa Senani's Nritta Ratnavali covers Perini in its seventh chapter, including the dancer's qualities, make-up and ornaments. It says dancers wore shell or gold ornaments, applied ash, tied the hair up and held a dummy cobra or wand in one hand and a fly whisk in the other.

The music named by Narthaki includes the mukhaveena, mridangam, nadaswaram, talas and sruti. The repertoire has items such as Gargharam, Geetham, and a closing Pancha Mukha Sabdam Nartanam in honour of Shiva.
Performers are described as warriors of Veera Shaiva sects who danced before battle. Narthaki adds that some texts mention women dancers, though one author treats Perini as a male domain.
artist: The key person in its modern story is Dr Nataraja Ramakrishna (31 March 1923 to 7 June 2011), a dancer, scholar and musicologist. He reconstructed Perini from the Nritta Ratnavali and the sculptures at Ramappa temple. Narthaki says he trained about 100 students.
His honours, per Narthaki, include the Padma Shri (1992) and election as Sangeet Natak Akademi Fellow in January 2011. Narthaki also says he added some entertainment elements to the revival.
The historical author of the text, Jayapa Senani, was an elephant commander under the Kakatiya king Ganapati-deva.
place: The Kakatiyas ruled from Warangal. The Ramalingeswara temple at Palampet, about 77 km from Warangal, is called the Ramappa temple after its chief sculptor. Its sculptures show dances from the Nritta Ratnavali.
Narthaki says Kakatiya-era performances took place in temples, sometimes before King Pratapa Rudra and Queen Rudramma Devi.

history.what: Perini flourishes under the Kakatiya rulers. Another source says its peak was in the 11th century, so sources differ.
Jayapa Senani serves the Kakatiya king Ganapati-deva (Wikipedia).
The date given by Narthaki for the Nritta Ratnavali. Wikipedia's Jayapa page gives his years in office up to 1235, so dates for the text are uncertain.
Wikipedia says the dance nearly disappeared.
Dr Nataraja Ramakrishna revives it from the text and the sculptures.
Wikipedia records a government-organised performance at Gajwel.

future: Training: train more dancers, including women, with Ramakrishna's students as teachers.
Livelihood: regular paid performances at Warangal and Ramappa.
Materials: keep drums and costume ornaments made by local craftspeople.
Documentation: film the repertoire and link each item to the text and sculpture.
Protection: record the lineage of Ramakrishna's students so the teaching chain is not lost.

name: Pulikali
tagline: Men painted as tigers dance through Thrissur on the fourth day of Onam.
facts: Held on the fourth day of Onam in Thrissur
Body paint takes five to seven hours
Teams called sanghams compete
Music: chenda and chengila
art: Pulikali means tiger play. Dancers are painted as tigers and perform in a procession that enacts the hunt. Scenes include a tiger preying on an animal and a tiger being hunted.

Wikipedia says the body is given two coats of paint, which takes five to seven hours. Modern costumes add masks, artificial teeth, beards and belts of small bells. Dancers shake their bellies to the beat of the chenda and chengila.
The groups also bring floats, and troupes compete for the best float and best-dressed tigers.
artist: The performers belong to teams called sanghams from across Thrissur. Each offers a coconut at the Ganapati shrine before circling the ground. Wikipedia says men and children usually perform. In 2016, three women joined a 51-member troupe for the first time.
Wikipedia says the Thrissur Municipal Corporation gives each troupe a grant of Rs 30,000. The Pulikali Coordination Committee, formed in 2004, organises the event.
I found no reliable named individual artists.
place: The main event is at Swaraj Round in Thrissur, on the fourth day of Onam (Vishakham in Chingam).
Thrissur is a temple town known for its Pooram festival, but Pulikali is a separate public celebration of Onam.

history.what: Wikipedia credits Rama Varma Sakthan Thampuran of Cochin with introducing it as Pulikkettikali. Its infobox gives 1886, so dates conflict.
The Pulikali Coordination Committee is formed.
Three women join a troupe for the first time.
A group live-streams a small performance because of COVID-19.

future: Support the painters and mask makers who prepare the tigers.
Use safe, skin-friendly paints, since the current ones are enamel and varnish.
Cover the high cost of team costumes with fair public grants.
Record the history of each sangham.
Make room for women and younger performers.

name: Raut Nacha
tagline: The Yadav cowherds' stick dance, sung in couplets after Diwali.
facts: Danced by the Raut (Yadav) community
Linked to Krishna and to Dev Uthani Ekadashi
Around Diwali; Bilaspur's festival lasts about 15 days
Music: dhol, nishan and other drums, with sung dohas
art: Raut Nacha is danced by the Raut, or Yadav, community of Chhattisgarh as a form of worship to Krishna. Wikipedia says it is performed around Dev Uthani Ekadashi, the day when the gods are believed to wake from their rest. Other sources place it after Diwali or on Govardhan puja.

One student source from the University of Hong Kong says the dancers carry sticks and metal shields, wear bright clothes, and act out Krishna's fight with Kansa, as a sign of good over evil. We have not found a second source for this reading, so take it as one account.
The dancing goes with dohas, short rhymed couplets. Sahapedia has an article by P. C. Lal Yadav on Raut dohas, with a focus on couplets about childhood.

The People's Archive of Rural India (PARI) describes Raut families in Achhoti in Durg district hiring gana-baja bands from Odisha for the Diwali period. These bands play dhap, dhol, jhanj, mahuri, nishan and tasha, and the nishan, a drum of leather and iron, is central. The dancers use a stick as they dance.
artist: The dancers belong to the Raut community; the sources we read do not describe individual dancers. PARI describes the Raut as an OBC (Other Backward Class) community. In villages, the group chooses and pays a band, with prices set by the days of play.
The musicians are a second community of artists. In Achhoti the gana-baja bands came from Odisha, and the Raut tested troupes before choosing one, PARI reports.
We did not find reliable names of individual Raut Nacha dancers or gurus.
place: Raut Nacha is danced across the Chhattisgarh plain, Sahapedia notes that Bilaspur holds a Raut Naach festival each year, organised around Diwali and lasting 15 days.
In the village, the dance moves through lanes and courtyards, and for the community the days of Govardhan puja and Gauri-Gaura puja are the heart of the season.

history.what: The origin of Raut Nacha is not documented in the sources we read. Folk accounts link it to Krishna and the Yadavas.
Danced after Diwali, around Dev Uthani Ekadashi and Govardhan puja.
Bilaspur holds a yearly Raut Naach festival of about 15 days around Diwali (Sahapedia). The start date of the Bilaspur festival is not given in the sources we read.

future: Record the dohas with the singers, with a Hindi or English gloss, before older singers are gone.
Pay dancers and bands for performances at festivals, not only at the village event.
Support the Odisha gana-baja musicians who play for the dancers, and document their repertoire.
Teach boys and girls the dance in schools in the Raut villages.
Make a plain-language archive of costume, steps and songs with the community's consent.

name: Rouf
tagline: Women in two facing rows, arms linked, singing their own accompaniment: one step forward, one back.
facts: Women's folk dance of Kashmir
No instruments; the dancers sing
Danced for Ramzan, Eid and weddings
Now seen mostly at weddings
art: Rouf is a dance of Kashmiri women. Daily Excelsior says no instruments are used. The dancers sing traditional songs themselves, on love, the beauty of Kashmir, happiness, sadness and devotion.

The Kashmir Walla describes women standing side by side, arms around each other's shoulders, moving in step, one step forward and one step back. Daily Excelsior describes two facing rows, holding hands or linking arms, with soft, matched steps.

Dancers wear the pheran, the long, often embroidered Kashmiri dress, with traditional jewellery. The songs were written by poets for particular occasions, and the Kashmir Walla mentions a street vendor who sold booklets of rouf songs that girls bought eagerly.
artist: Rouf belongs to ordinary women. The Kashmir Walla speaks with Dilshad Ara, 65, of Srinagar's Karan Nagar, who has danced and sung rouf for decades, and with younger women, Samrah Mir and Sadaf Zahra, who say people now feel shy of the tradition.

Dr. Aziz Hajini, a former Secretary of the Jammu and Kashmir Cultural Academy, argues that writing it down keeps Kashmiri cultural identity alive. Some women told the writer they were told as girls that they should not dance.
Young women show little interest in learning it, the article says.
place: Rouf is danced across the Kashmir Valley. The Kashmir Walla speaks to women in Srinagar. We did not find a source naming a single village as its home.
It belongs to the Valley's calendar. Women danced through Ramzan, on the eve of Eid, on Bakrid and at weddings, says the Kashmir Walla. Daily Excelsior adds the arrival of spring.

history.what: None of the pages we could open says where or when rouf began, so we give no date.
Women performed it throughout Ramzan, to mark its start and later to celebrate Eid, and on the eve of Eid before the festive family meal, according to the Kashmir Walla.
It is now mostly limited to weddings, and cultural programmes and festivals, the two articles say.

future: Training: let older women who know the songs teach girls in community and school settings.
Livelihood: pay and credit the women who perform it at weddings, festivals and cultural events.
Materials: collect the song booklets and the old texts, with the poets' names where known.
Documentation: record the songs and steps in video and writing, as Dr. Hajini urges, with the singers' permission.
Protection: make room for women to dance and teach without shame.

name: Sattriya
tagline: A monastery dance made by the saint Sankardeva, once danced only by monks before a holy book.
facts: Form: devotional dance from Vaishnava monasteries (satras)
Linked to Sankardeva, 15th to 16th century
Basic exercises called mati akhora
Recognised by Sangeet Natak Akademi in 2000
art: Sattriya is a dance of the satras, the Vaishnava monasteries of Assam. Wikipedia says it began as part of bhaona, the dramatic performances of Ankiya Nat, one-act plays by Sankardeva. A dance in which the story is told in front of a copy of the Bhagavata Purana, not an idol.

It has pure dance (nritta), expressive dance (nritya) and dramatic play (natya). The basic training steps are called mati akhora. Music includes the borgeets, songs set to ragas by Sankardeva and Madhavadeva, along with the khol drum, cymbals and flute.
The style is calm and devotional. Many items are ritual parts of the satra day, such as dances of the opening and closing of a service.
In the satras it was traditionally danced by the monks (bhokots). It is now also performed on stage by men and women.
artist: Sankardeva, a saint, poet and playwright of the 15th and 16th centuries, began the neo-Vaishnava movement in Assam. His principal disciple, Madhavadeva, worked with him to write and direct the early plays, mostly composed in the 16th century, according to Wikipedia.

For centuries the dance was kept inside the satras by monks, who trained in the mati akhora, the gayan-bayan (singers and instrumentalists) and the bhaona. The monks were both performers and caretakers of the satra.

In the 20th century, dancers brought it out to the public stage, and in 2000 the Sangeet Natak Akademi recognised it as one of India's classical dances. Individual names in the revival, such as Maniram Dutta Muktiyar and Indira P. P. Bora, are mentioned in other accounts, which I did not check in time.
Our approach: let the satra monks (bhokots) speak for their own tradition, and name satras and teachers carefully.
place: Assam lies along the Brahmaputra. Majuli, the river island of the Brahmaputra in upper Assam, is a main centre of the neo-Vaishnava culture. Wikipedia says Sankardeva's followers founded 65 satras there, of which only 23 remain active.
Majuli is also home to the Mising, Deori and Sonowal Kachari communities, and to craft traditions such as mask-making and pottery in the satras. Reaching the island needs a ferry from Jorhat.

The island is shrinking. Wikipedia reports that its area fell from about 1,300 square km in the 1790s to about 880 square km by 2024, and more than 35 villages have been washed away since 1991. Satras and their dance traditions are therefore tied to a threatened landscape.

history.what: Sankardeva and Madhavadeva compose plays, songs and dances for the satras. Exact dates of the saint are still discussed in the sources.
Satras spread across Assam, and on Majuli in particular. Sattriya develops as a monastery tradition.
Satra life continues under the Ahom kings, and dance remains inside the satras. Details vary in sources.
Dancers and scholars begin to teach and perform Sattriya outside the satras.
The Sangeet Natak Akademi recognises Sattriya as one of India's classical dances.
Erosion by the Brahmaputra shrinks Majuli, and many villages are washed away.

future: Protect Majuli and its satras from erosion, and help satras move or rebuild when needed, with the monks' consent.
Record the ritual dances, borgeets and khol playing of each satra with the bhokots, before elders pass on.
Fund training places for young monks and for outside students, with scholarships for children from the island's communities.
Support khol makers, mask makers and costume weavers who supply the satras.
Create respectful visitor guidelines for Majuli, so tourism supports the satras and does not disturb worship.
Keep a public archive of Ankiya Nat, borgeets and bhaona texts in Assamese with translations.

name: Sikkimese Cham Masks
tagline: Painted masks worn by monks to dance the victory of good over evil.
facts: Cham is a masked dance performed in monasteries
Kagyed Cham honours eight Tantric deities
Held on the 28th and 29th days of the 10th Tibetan month
Masks: softwood, clay and paper pulp
art: Cham is a lively masked and costumed dance of Tibetan Buddhism. Wikipedia says many chams show episodes from the life of Padmasambhava, and that they are considered meditation and an offering to the gods. They often teach compassion and bring merit to those who watch.

Sikkim's craft department says the masks were once made only in monasteries and are now also made by local people. They are of softwood, clay and paper pulp, and show gods, goddesses and animals with calm or angry faces, painted in yellow, blue, green, orange or white. Masks are now also sold as wall hangings.

Kagyed Cham is performed in the name of eight Tantric deities and tells episodes from Buddhist mythology, especially the life of Guru Padmasambhava, according to Windhorse Tours. Monks wear masks, costumes and ceremonial swords. The festival closes with the burning of effigies of flour, wood and paper.
artist: Dancers are monks. The craft department notes cham is performed by lamas in monasteries. We could not confirm from a source we read who performs other Sikkim cham festivals, and sources we saw differ on whether lay youths take part in some.
Makers were first monastery artists and now include local craftspeople, the craft department says. We did not find a source we could read that names individual mask makers.
place: Windhorse Tours says Kagyed Cham is celebrated at Old Rumtek Monastery, Phodong Monastery and the Tshuklakhang (Palace Monastery) in Gangtok. It falls on the 28th and 29th day of the 10th Tibetan month, usually December, two days before Losoong, the Sikkimese New Year.
The dance is read as a symbol of victory. Lamas pray for protection from evil spirits, and watchers are believed to receive blessings.

history.what: Padmasambhava, a 9th-century teacher, appears as a subject of many cham dances, according to Wikipedia.
One cham, performed before Losar, recalls the killing of King Langdarma by the monk Lhalung Pelgyi Dorje, per Wikipedia. The story is read as the victory of good over evil.
Wikipedia notes that the label devil dance came from Western views of the costumes.
Mask making moved from monasteries to local craftspeople, per the Sikkim craft department.

future: Training: support young monks and mask painters to learn the steps and the craft.
Livelihood: fair pay for mask makers, especially for wall-hanging and souvenir markets.
Materials: keep supplies of softwood, clay and paper pulp.
Documentation: record each monastery's cham, its characters and its masks.
Protection: keep the sacred meaning clear when masks are sold or shown to visitors.

name: Singhi Chham
tagline: The snow lion dance, in honour of Kanchenjunga.
facts: Also called the Kanchendzonga Dance
Two to four snow lions, each worn by two men
One drummer accompanies
Belongs to the Bhutia people
art: Singhi Chham is a lion dance of Sikkim, also called the Kanchendzonga Dance. Wikipedia says the dancers wear a white lion costume with a bluish mane, representing the snow lion. Two to four lions perform, and each is worn by two men. A single drummer accompanies the dance.
The dance has religious meaning. Kanchenjunga, a peak sacred to the Sikkimese, is believed to resemble the legendary snow lion, the article says, though that claim carries no citation there.
artist: Wikipedia describes the dance as belonging to the Bhutia people. We did not find a source we could read that names individual dancers or teachers.
place: The dance is usually performed at the Pang Lhabsol festival, says Wikipedia, which does not give a source for that. Sikkim's cham tradition is held at monasteries such as Rumtek and Phodong and at the Tshuklakhang in Gangtok, per Windhorse Tours, though that page is about Kagyed Cham, not this dance.

history.what: Wikipedia says the dance is said to have been introduced by Chador Namgyal, the third Chogyal of Sikkim, in the 18th century. It cites a web page, so treat this as tradition.
Cham dances in general belong to Tibetan Buddhism and are meant as offering and meditation, per Wikipedia.

future: Training: young dancers and drummers learning from experienced performers.
Livelihood: pay for performers and costume makers during festivals.
Documentation: record the dance, music and costume in detail, as little was found.
Protection: keep the festival context, and let communities say how the dance is shown.

name: Tarpa Dance
states: Dadra and Nagar Haveli and Daman and Diu
tagline: Dancers circle around one player of a gourd-and-bamboo pipe, in the nights after the harvest.
facts: Form: circle dance led by a tarpa (wind instrument) player
Danced by Warli communities; some sources add Kokna and Koli
Season: after the monsoon harvest, to Diwali
Tarpa player at the centre is a common Warli painting motif
art: The tarpa dance is a group dance of the tribal communities of Dadra and Nagar Haveli. Dancers form a circle, or a spiral, around a musician who plays the tarpa. They often hold each other by the waist or hand so that the line moves as one chain.

The tarpa is a wind instrument made from forest materials. Wikipedia, which itself warns of weak sourcing, describes a dried bottle gourd as the wind chest, two bamboo pipes with reeds, and a flared horn made of folded dried palm leaves, with beeswax as the seal. It can be between about two and six feet long. The player keeps up a drone and a melody together and needs controlled breathing to do so.

The dancers follow the player. As the tune changes, the circle changes pace and shape. Sources say performances begin around sunset and may go on until dawn. Treat that as a general description: I found no field study of the dance in Silvassa itself.
Sources differ on who dances it. Some name the Warli. Other general sites add the Koli and Kokna.
artist: The central artist is the tarpa player. The instrument is usually played solo, and the whole circle depends on the player's breath and tune. The instrument is handmade, and the gourd is sometimes painted.

The dancers are ordinary village men and women, and the dance is part of community life rather than a stage art. The Tribal Museum page lists the Varli (Warli), Dhodia, Kokna and Kathodia tribes of the territory.

Some writers say the Warli believe a deity gave them the tarpa. This comes from tribal lore reported by secondary writers, so it is a belief to be attributed and not a proven fact. I did not find named tarpa players from Dadra and Nagar Haveli in any source I could read.
place: Dadra and Nagar Haveli lie inland of the Gujarat coast, in forest and hill country close to the Maharashtra border. Silvassa is the capital and the place where visitors most often meet the tribal arts. The Tribal Museum there shows the lives of the Varli, Dhodia, Kokna and Kathodi communities through ornaments, musical instruments, fishing and hunting tools and farm tools.

The tarpa and its dance are shared across a wider Warli belt in Maharashtra and Gujarat, so this is a regional art and not a single village's tradition. The territory was merged with Daman and Diu in 2020.

history.what: No source I read dates the tarpa dance. It is described as a long-standing tribal tradition, and no firm date is known.
Wikipedia describes the tarpa as the main instrument, with the dhol, at Warli gatherings and marriages. It carries a warning about reliance on self-published sources.
The dance is tied to the post-monsoon harvest, from the harvest until Diwali, and is also reported at Holi and weddings by secondary sources.
The tarpa player in a circle of dancers is a frequent motif in Warli painting. An auction-house blog says so, but its larger claims about meaning are not backed by scholarship.
The territory was merged with Daman and Diu, as reported by Wikipedia's page on Diu.

future: Record tarpa players and their repertoires on audio and video, with the village and community named, and keep the files with the territory's tribal museum.
Pay tarpa makers and players for demonstrations in schools and festivals, so young people see the work as a livelihood.
Help makers get gourd, bamboo and palm leaf in good quality, and write down how the instrument is built.
Hold the dance in its own season and village, with visitors invited in as guests, not moved to a stage.
Ask the communities themselves, not outside writers, to say what the dance means.

pins.label: Silvassa, capital of Dadra and Nagar Haveli

name: Theyyam
tagline: A ritual in which the performer, in a towering crown and red face paint, becomes the god.
facts: Form: ritual worship, also called Kaliyattam
Region: North Malabar (Kannur, Kasaragod)
Season: about mid-October to late May
Hundreds of forms, over a hundred well known
art: Theyyam is a ritual of worship, not a stage show. People of North Malabar believe the god (Daivam) comes down among them and enters the performer. Kerala Tourism describes it as a divine power that descends among the people and protects the land.

The preparation is long. Wikipedia says it runs about eight to ten hours and ends when the headgear, the mudi, is placed on the performer. That moment marks the entry of the deity. The mudi can be very tall and is described by Kerala Tourism as the most important part of the costume.

The face is painted in natural colours such as rice flour, turmeric and charcoal, and red is the main colour, standing for energy and anger. Costumes use coconut-frond and areca-leaf skirts, wooden breastplates and masks, depending on the deity. Each Theyyam has its own face design, dress, song and dance.

There are very many Theyyams: sources count roughly 400 forms, of which around a hundred are well known. Examples named by Kerala Tourism include Muchilottu Bhagavathy and Kathivannur Veeran. Wikipedia also lists Muthappan, Vishnumoorthy and Gulikan. They include goddesses, heroes, tree and forest spirits, and even Muslim figures such as Bappiriyan and Ummachi.
It is performed outdoors, in front of village shrines, family shrines and sacred groves, with no stage or curtain.
artist: Kerala Tourism says the performers are mainly from the Malayan and Vannan communities, both Scheduled Castes, along with some other small communities. Wikipedia adds that members of Thiyya communities carry out certain rites.

Before a performance the artist follows a strict discipline called vrutham, with fasting, prayer and meditation. Writers note that caste still shapes the performers' daily lives, and one Caravan report quotes a senior practitioner who would not call it simply anti-caste.

For much of the year many performers work other jobs. Press reports mention auto-rickshaw driving, well-digging and toddy tapping. When the Covid-19 lockdown cancelled the season, many lost their main income.
Our approach: speak with the families who perform, and let them decide what is shown to outsiders and what stays within the shrine.
place: Theyyam belongs to the north of Kerala, mainly Kannur and Kasaragod, with some performance in Wayanad, northern Kozhikode and nearby parts of Karnataka. This is the old Malabar country, on the Arabian Sea coast with the Western Ghats behind it.

The season starts about the tenth day of the month of Thulam (mid-October) and runs to the middle of Edavam (late May). Kerala Tourism gives this range; some sources say the season ends into June. It follows the dry months after the monsoon. Shrines in Kasaragod tend to hold their festivals first, and the season moves south through Kannur. Wikipedia says it closes at the Madayi Kavu and Kalarivathukkal temples.

Many Theyyams are held in kavu, small sacred groves or shrine compounds. A grove keeps old trees standing in a landscape of paddy and coconut, so the ritual and the ecology are linked. Sources I consulted did not give a full account of how many groves survive, which needs local research.
Visitors come for the season, which brings both income and the risk of treating a ritual as a spectacle.

history.what: Wikipedia suggests the tradition may go back to ancestor worship and to older tribal and village cults. Scholars do not agree on a date.
Many Theyyams honour heroes, ancestors and local goddesses. Researchers disagree on how and when individual Theyyams arose.
Patronage and social change have altered how shrines and performers are supported. Sources I consulted do not give a clear timeline.
The Kerala Folklore Academy was set up by the state government to promote folk art forms, including Theyyam.
A senior Theyyam artist from Kannur received a Kerala Folklore Academy fellowship, as reported by The Caravan.
The Covid-19 lockdown halted the season and left many performers without income, as reported by Deccan Herald.
Theyyam is a feature of Kerala Tourism's northern circuit, and scholars are studying performers' health and livelihoods.

future: Support Theyyam families with health cover and a safety net, since the work is physically heavy and the season is short.
Document the songs (thottam) and ritual knowledge with the performers' consent, and return copies to the families.
Protect kavu groves: community mapping, tree cover and local committees with a say in how tourism is run.
Set simple visitor rules: no interruption of rites, respectful dress and distance, and fair, direct payment to performers.
Help young performers in the community stay in school and still learn the craft, including costume and headgear making.
Keep a calendar of festivals in local hands so that visitors come to the community, not over it.

name: Wangala and Nongkrem Dances
tagline: Long drums for the Garo sun god, and swords and white whisks for the Khasi harvest prayer.
facts: Wangala: Garo harvest festival for Saljong, the sun god; also called the Hundred Drums festival
Nongkrem: five-day Khasi religious festival at Smit, usually in November
Wangala drums are long, oval drums called dama
Nongkrem men dance with a sword and a white yak-hair whisk
art: Two harvest-time dances of Meghalaya are told together here. Wangala belongs to the Garo people. Nongkrem belongs to the Khasi people. Both are tied to prayer as much as to performance.

Wangala marks the end of the work in the fields and the coming of winter. The Meghalaya government page says it honours Saljong, the sun god of fertility, with offerings. Wikipedia names the deity Misi Saljong. The festival opens with a ceremony in the house of the village chief, the Nokma. There a priest called the Kamal pours rice beer (Rugala) and burns incense. Then comes the dancing.

Dancers wear bright clothes and feathered headgear. Men and women form two parallel lines and move forward in rhythm, while men beat long, oval drums called dama. Flutes, gongs and a flute made of buffalo horn add to the sound. Dama Gogata, the drum dance, is performed on the last day. Wikipedia lists other items too, such as Katta Doka, Dani Doka and the Pomelo Dance (Chambil Mesaa).

Nongkrem, or Pomblang Nongkrem, is a five-day Khasi religious festival. Sources say it gives thanks for the harvest and prays for peace and prosperity. The Syiem of Khyrim and the high priest perform the Pomblang rites, which include goat sacrifice, and offerings go to Lei Shyllong, the deity of Shillong peak, and to the ancestors of the ruling clan. The government page says the festival honours the goddess Ka Blei Synshar.

After the rites come the dances. Unmarried girls dance in traditional costume. The men dance more vigorously, holding a sword in the right hand and a white yak-hair whisk in the left. Drums keep the beat and the tangmuri pipes are played. One tourism page says the women are the central figures of the dance and the men move around them as protectors. I found that reading in one source only.
artist: These dances belong to whole communities, not to named performers. In Wangala the Nokma, the village chief, hosts the opening rites, and the Kamal, a priest, performs them. Men drum and men and women dance.

Wangala is kept most closely in Songsarek villages, where people follow the old Garo religion. Wikipedia names Sadolpara in West Garo Hills as an example. The large Hundred Drums festival at Asanang invites performers who may or may not be Christian. Wikipedia says students of Christian Girls' Higher Secondary School in Tura take part, as dance is part of their curriculum.

In Nongkrem the ruling clan of Khyrim has the central role. The Syiem (the traditional ruler) and the high priest lead the rites. Unmarried girls and young men carry the dance. I did not find the names of any individual dancers or teachers in the sources I read.
place: The Garo Hills lie in western Meghalaya, with Tura as the main town. The Hundred Drums Wangala was first held on 6 and 7 December 1976 at Asanang, about 18 km from Tura, according to news and Wikipedia reports. Villages traditionally set their own dates, between September and December. The state tourism page puts it in the first week of November.

Nongkrem is held at Smit, the seat of the Khyrim Syiemship in the Khasi Hills. Sources put Smit between 11 and 15 km from Shillong. The main venue is the Ing Sad, a thatched building. The festival is usually in November, though one source says October or November. In 2023 the East Khasi Hills administration declared a local holiday for it.

history.what: Wangala is a village harvest rite. Two or three neighbouring villages celebrate together for two to three days, or up to a week.
Sources I read do not give a documented origin for Wangala or Nongkrem. The Wikipedia history section on Wangala has no citations.
The first Hundred Drums Wangala is held at Asanang, near Tura, and has run every year since, according to news reports.
The Asanang festival grows to include troupes from outside the Garo Hills. Wikipedia says these include Bangladesh and Karbi Anglong, and that prize money is offered.
Nongkrem is held at Smit over five days, led by the Syiem of Khyrim and the high priest.
East Khasi Hills declares a local holiday for Nongkrem on 2 November, per a government circular.
Goalpara in Assam hosts its first Wangala festival on 7 and 8 November, per a news report. Wikipedia notes Garo communities also live in Assam, Nagaland and Bangladesh.

future: Training: village elders, and school and college troupes, pass on the steps and drum rhythms. Dance is already taught in some schools in Tura.
Livelihood: crowds at Asanang and Smit bring work for musicians, costume makers and food sellers. Prize money and tourism help, but should not turn rites into pure shows.
Materials: dama drums, feather headgear, swords and whisks are made by hand. Records of who makes them, and where materials come from, are thin.
Documentation: audio and video of the Songsarek form of Wangala and of the Nongkrem rites, made with community consent, would help.
Protection: care is needed to keep sacred rites with the priests and chiefs who hold them, even as the public dances reach wider audiences.
